MODULES.title: What AI Actually Is
MODULES.tag: LLMs demystified: a text-prediction machine, not a mind
MODULES.why: Almost everything people call "AI" today runs on the same kind of engine: a large language model. If you understand what that engine really does, and the few things it can't do, you'll stop being surprised by it. You'll know when to trust it, when to double-check it, and why it behaves the way it does. Every other lesson in this course builds on this one idea.
MODULES.mental: A large language model is a text-prediction machine. You give it some text, and it guesses the most likely next chunk of text, over and over, until it has written a full answer. That's the whole trick. On its own, the model isn't looking anything up, it has no memory of you, and it isn't "thinking" the way a person does. (Apps add searching and memory around this engine, and their "thinking" modes are this same engine writing out working notes before it answers. You'll meet each of these later in the course.) Once you picture it as a very, very well-read autocomplete, the rest of AI stops feeling like magic and starts feeling like a tool with rules.
concepts: LLM (large language model)

The engine behind ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. It's a program trained on an enormous amount of text, and its one job is to predict what text comes next. That simple skill, done extremely well, is enough to write, summarize, answer questions, and even code.
Predicting the next word

When you ask the model something, it builds its answer one piece at a time, each time guessing the most likely next piece based on everything so far. Nothing is written in advance, the whole answer is assembled on the spot.
Training

Before you ever use it, the model was shown a huge amount of text and slowly tuned to get better at predicting it. Then came a second round, often called fine-tuning, on example conversations, human feedback, and practice problems with checkable answers, which turns a raw text-predictor into a helpful assistant. All of this happened in advance: chatting with the model doesn't change it. (Companies do train newer versions later, sometimes using people's chats if their settings allow it.)
It sounds confident either way
Because the model's goal is to produce text that reads well, it phrases a wrong answer just as smoothly as a right one. Confidence in the wording tells you nothing about whether it's correct.
Not a search engine

A search engine finds existing pages and shows them to you. A language model doesn't look anything up on its own, it generates new text from patterns it learned. That's why it can be creative, and also why it can make things up. (Many apps bolt a search step on top; you'll meet that in the tools lesson.)
Same engine, many products

ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all chat products built on top of large language models. The chat window, memory, web search, and voice features are extras built around that core text-prediction engine, which is why the same kind of engine can feel so different from one app to the next.
"Thinking" is still prediction

Some apps offer a "thinking" or reasoning mode. The model hasn't become a mind: it writes out working notes first (breaking the problem down, trying an approach, checking it) and then writes the answer. The notes are predicted text too, but they give a hard, multi-step problem room to be worked through, which is why thinking modes are slower and noticeably better at math, planning, and tricky analysis.
mistakes: Thinking the model "knows" things the way a database does, it's predicting likely text, not retrieving stored facts
Trusting an answer because it sounds confident, fluent wording and correctness are unrelated
Expecting the model itself to remember past conversations, it doesn't; any carry-over comes from an app's memory feature, covered later
Assuming it searched the web, the model can't on its own; many apps add a search step, so look for sources to know whether one actually ran
Treating it as a calculator for exact math or precise quotes, it predicts plausible text, which isn't the same as being exact
flags: "The AI told me, so it must be right", confidence isn't evidence; verify anything that matters
"It made up a fact / a fake quote / a broken link", that's the prediction engine filling a gap, not a glitch you can fully turn off
"It forgot what I said earlier", you likely hit the limits of its short-term memory, covered in the context lesson
"It gave me a different answer the second time", normal, the model makes fresh guesses each time
ask: Is this a question where being wrong would cost me, and if so, how will I check the answer?
Am I expecting it to recall something, or to generate something? (It's much better at generating.)
Could this need fresh or private information the model was never trained on?
Would a real source (a search, a document, a person) be a better fit than a confident guess?

MODULES.title: Tokens & How Models Read Text
MODULES.tag: The model doesn't read words, it reads tokens, and that explains a lot
MODULES.why: AI is priced in tokens, you run out of room in tokens, and a few of the model's weirdest quirks (bad spelling tricks, shaky math, trouble counting letters) come straight from tokens. You don't need to count them by hand, but once you know what a token is, three confusing things about AI suddenly make sense: why it costs what it costs, why it sometimes forgets, and why it stumbles on tasks that look easy.
MODULES.mental: Before the model can predict the next chunk of text, it has to chop your text into pieces. Those pieces are called tokens. A token is usually a short run of characters, often about three-quarters of a word, so common words are one token, and longer or unusual words get split into several. The model never sees letters or whole words the way you do, it sees a stream of tokens. Picture it reading text in puzzle pieces rather than letters: that one image explains the cost, the limits, and the quirks you'll meet for the rest of this course.
concepts: Token

The small chunk of text a model actually reads and writes. Often a common word, a word-piece, a space, or a punctuation mark. As a rough rule of thumb, one token is about four characters of English, or roughly three-quarters of a word. The exact split varies from model to model, so the same text can come out as a different number of tokens in two different apps.
Tokenizing
The step where your text is sliced into tokens before the model sees it. It happens automatically, every time, for both what you send in and what the model writes back.
Why splitting helps

There are too many possible words (and typos, and names) to give each its own slot. Breaking text into a fixed set of reusable pieces, often a hundred thousand or more, lets the model handle any text, even words it never saw, by spelling them out of smaller pieces.
Tokens, not words, are the unit

Length limits and pricing are measured in tokens, not words or characters. A long word can be several tokens, and a space or comma can be its own token, so token counts rarely match word counts exactly.
Input tokens and output tokens
Everything you send (your question, plus any text you paste in) is input tokens. Everything the model writes back is output tokens. Both count, and longer of either means slower and more expensive.
Where the quirks come from

Because the model sees tokens, not letters, tasks that depend on individual characters get hard: counting the letters in a word, reversing it, or precise spelling. It's not that the model is dumb here, it just isn't looking at letters.
Pictures and files count too
Images, audio, and attached files get turned into tokens as well, so a big screenshot, a long recording, or a fat PDF uses up room and cost just like a wall of pasted text.
"Thinking" uses tokens too

When a model works through a problem before answering, those working notes are output tokens, even when you never see them. That's a big part of why thinking modes are slower and use more of your budget or usage limits.
mistakes: Assuming one word equals one token, short common words are one token, but longer or rarer words split into several, so counts don't line up
Forgetting that the text you paste in counts too, a long document you attach can use far more tokens than your actual question
Being surprised the model miscounts letters or botches a word-reversal, it reads tokens, not letters, so character-level tasks are genuinely its weak spot
Thinking only your input is billed, the answer the model writes (output tokens) costs too, and is often the bigger half
Expecting other languages to cost the same, text in many non-English languages splits into more tokens, so the same meaning can cost more
flags: "Why did this short chat cost so much?", you probably pasted in a long document; that input is tokens too
"It can't tell me how many r's are in a word", classic token blind spot, it isn't seeing the letters
"It cut off mid-answer", you likely hit a length limit measured in tokens, covered next lesson on the context window
"The same request is pricier in my language", some languages tokenize into more pieces, so they cost more for the same content
ask: Am I about to paste in a lot of text? If so, that's a lot of tokens, do I really need all of it?
Is this a letter-by-letter task (counting characters, exact spelling, reversing a word)? If so, the model may struggle, and a simple tool would be more reliable.
Could I get the same result with a shorter prompt or a shorter requested answer, to save time and cost?
If cost matters, have I checked roughly how many tokens my typical request uses?

MODULES.title: The Context Window
MODULES.tag: The model's short-term memory, and why it's smaller than you think
MODULES.why: This one idea explains the single most common frustration people have with AI: "why did it forget what I just told it?" The model can only look at a limited amount of text at once, called the context window. Everything it knows in the moment, your question, the conversation so far, any file you pasted, has to fit inside that window. Understand the window and you'll know why long chats drift, why pasting a giant document can backfire, and how to keep the model on track.
MODULES.mental: The model has no memory of its own between messages. Each time you hit send, it's handed one big block of text, the conversation so far plus your new message, and it reads only that. The size limit on that block is the context window. Think of it as the model's desk, not its filing cabinet: only what's on the desk right now can be used, and the desk has an edge. When the conversation grows past that edge, the oldest things slide off and are simply gone. The model isn't choosing to forget, it literally never sees what fell off the desk.
concepts: Context window

The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, the model can look at in one go. It has to hold everything at once: the conversation history, your current message, any pasted files, and the answer being written.
It's the model's working memory
Whatever is in the window is what the model 'knows' in this moment. It doesn't remember earlier chats, and within a chat it only has what still fits in the window right now.
Falling off the edge

When a conversation gets longer than the window, something has to give. Depending on the app, the earliest messages are dropped, squeezed into a short summary, or you're asked to start a new chat. Either way, details from early on can be lost, because from the model's point of view they're no longer there in full.
Bigger windows, real limits

Modern models have large windows (often enough for hundreds of pages, sometimes several whole books), but the limit is still real, still measured in tokens, and using a big window is slower and costs more.
More text isn't always better

Stuffing the window with everything you have can actually hurt, the important detail gets buried in noise and the model may latch onto the wrong thing. Engineers even have a name for how accuracy slips as the window fills up: context rot. A focused, relevant context usually beats a huge one.
When it can't all fit, the app may search

Give some apps more material than fits (a big project folder, a pile of documents) and they switch to searching it, pulling only the most relevant pieces onto the desk for each question. That's called retrieval. It's how you can 'chat with' far more than the window holds, and also why the model can miss a detail it never pulled in.
You control the window
You decide what goes in: a tight question with just the needed details, or a long ramble with a pasted novel. Curating what the model sees is the most practical skill in this whole course.
mistakes: Assuming the model remembers everything you've ever said to it, within a chat it only has what still fits the window, and across chats it remembers nothing by default
Pasting in a huge document and expecting laser-accurate recall, the more you cram in, the easier it is for the key detail to get lost
Blaming the model for 'forgetting' early parts of a very long conversation, those parts likely fell off the edge of the window
Thinking a bigger context window is always better, it costs more, runs slower, and can dilute the important bits
Burying the actual question at the top of a wall of text, the model does best when the ask is clear and the context around it is relevant
flags: "It forgot a detail I gave it ten messages ago", that detail probably slid off the edge of the window; restate it
"It's ignoring most of the long document I pasted", important parts may be buried; give it just the relevant section
"Long chats get worse over time", normal drift as early context drops off; starting a fresh chat with a clean summary often fixes it
"It mixed up two different things I asked about", too much unrelated stuff in the window at once; keep one task per conversation when it matters
"It summarized our chat and lost a detail", some apps condense older messages to make room; restate anything that must survive word for word
"It missed something in my uploaded files", with lots of material the app may search for pieces instead of reading it all; point it to the exact document or section
ask: Does the model actually have, in this conversation, the detail I'm expecting it to use? If not, I need to include it.
Am I giving it the relevant context, or just a lot of context? Could I trim this down to what matters?
Has this chat gotten really long? Would starting fresh with a short summary work better?
Is my real question easy to spot, or is it buried under everything I pasted?

MODULES.title: Talking to the Model: Prompting Basics
MODULES.tag: The words you give it are the steering wheel, small changes, big differences
MODULES.why: The same model can give you a vague, useless answer or a sharp, exactly-what-you-wanted one, and the only thing that changed was how you asked. That request you type is called a prompt, and learning to write a good one is the highest-leverage skill in this whole course. You don't need clever tricks or secret phrases. You need a few plain habits that get you from "meh" to "that's perfect" far more often.
MODULES.mental: A prompt is just the text you give the model to work with, and the model takes it completely literally, it can't read your mind, and it can't see your screen or your files unless you share them. So think of prompting as briefing a brilliant, eager new assistant on their first day: they're capable and fast, but they know nothing about your situation unless you tell them. The clearer you are about the task, the context, and what a good answer looks like, the better the result. A vague brief gets a vague reply, a specific brief gets a specific one. You're not casting a spell, you're writing a good set of instructions.
concepts: Prompt

The text you send the model, your question or instruction, plus any context or examples you include. It's the entire input the model has to work from, so whatever you leave out, it simply doesn't know.
Be specific about the task

Tell the model exactly what you want it to do. "Write something about dogs" and "Write a friendly three-sentence intro for a dog-walking flyer" produce very different results, because the second one actually says what success looks like.
Give it the context it needs

The model only knows what you tell it in the prompt. Who's the audience, what's the goal, what background matters? Including the relevant context is usually the difference between a generic answer and one that fits your situation.
Say what a good answer looks like
Ask for the format you want: a bulleted list, a short paragraph, a table, a specific tone, a length. The model is happy to oblige, but only if you say so, otherwise it guesses.
Show an example
If you have a sample of the style or format you want, paste it in and say "like this." One good example often teaches the model more than a paragraph of instructions.
Iterate, don't expect perfection first try

Prompting is a conversation. If the first answer is close but not right, tell it what to change ("shorter," "more formal," "focus on the second point"). Refining is normal and usually faster than rewriting from scratch.
mistakes: Being too vague, a one-line request with no context gets a generic answer, the model fills the gaps with guesses
Assuming the model can see what you see, unless you attach, share, or connect something, all it has is the words in your prompt
Not saying what format or length you want, then being annoyed it wrote five paragraphs when you wanted three bullets
Giving up after one mediocre answer instead of refining, the second or third pass is usually where it gets good
Piling on so many instructions at once that the important one gets lost, sometimes it's better to do it in steps
flags: "It gave me something generic and bland", the prompt was probably too vague; add the task, the audience, and the format you want
"It answered a slightly different question than I meant", it took your wording literally; restate the ask more precisely
"It's the right idea but the wrong shape", you likely didn't specify format or length; just ask for the shape you want
"It keeps missing one requirement", too much crammed in one prompt; pull that requirement out and handle it as its own step
ask: Have I actually said what I want, clearly enough that a stranger could follow it?
Does the model have the context it needs, or am I assuming it knows something I never told it?
Did I say what a good answer looks like, the format, length, and tone?
If the first answer is close, what one change would I ask for to make it right?

MODULES.title: How Chat Works
MODULES.tag: There's no "it" remembering you, just the same block of text, re-sent every turn
MODULES.why: Chatting with an AI feels like talking to someone who's following along. But under the hood, there's no "someone" keeping track, the chat is a clever illusion built on top of a model with no memory. Understanding how that illusion actually works clears up a surprising number of confusions: why a new chat starts blank, why "memory" features are a separate add-on, and why the model can suddenly contradict itself. Once you see the mechanism, you'll use chat tools with far less surprise.
MODULES.mental: The model itself is stateless, a fancy word for "it remembers nothing between turns." Each message you send, it sees fresh, with no recollection of the last one. So how does a conversation hold together? The chat app does the remembering for it. Every time you hit send, the app quietly re-sends the entire conversation so far, all of it, your messages and the model's replies, glued together, with your new message tacked on the end. The model reads that whole block, answers, and forgets again. Picture it as a brilliant expert with no memory, handed a complete transcript before every single reply. The continuity you feel isn't in the model, it's in the transcript the app keeps re-handing it.
concepts: Stateless

The model keeps no memory between turns. Each request is handled on its own, as if it were the first thing you'd ever said. Any sense of an ongoing conversation comes from outside the model, not from the model itself.
Conversation history
The running transcript of everything said so far, your messages and the model's replies. The chat app stores this and re-sends the whole thing each turn so the model has the full picture.
The illusion of memory

Because the app re-feeds the entire history every turn, the model appears to remember. It isn't, it's re-reading the transcript each time. Same effect, completely different mechanism, and the difference matters when things go wrong.
A new chat is a blank slate

Start a fresh conversation and you get a fresh transcript. Unless a memory feature slips in notes from before, the model knows nothing about your previous chats. That's not a bug, each chat is its own separate transcript.
"Memory" features are an extra layer

Many apps now have a memory feature, often switched on by default. It saves notes about you (and in some apps draws on your past chats) and slips them into the transcript automatically. That's a feature built on top of the model, not something the model does on its own, and you can usually view, edit, delete, or switch off what it keeps.
System message (the hidden brief)

Most chat tools quietly add an instruction at the very top of the transcript, before your first word, telling the model how to behave ("You are a helpful assistant") and often giving it today's date. You don't see it, but it's part of every turn, shaping the tone and rules of the whole chat.
Projects and custom instructions

Many apps let you write a standing brief once (about you, your preferences, or a project) and attach files to it. The app quietly adds that brief to the transcript of every chat in that space, a bit like your own system message. The model still isn't remembering; the app is re-sending your notes.
Temporary (incognito) chats

Most apps offer a chat that isn't saved to your history, doesn't feed the memory feature, and isn't used to train future models, handy for one-off or sensitive questions. The company may still keep it for a short time for safety checks, so it's more private, not invisible.
mistakes: Thinking the model is personally remembering you, it's the app re-sending the transcript; the model itself recalls nothing
Expecting a brand-new chat to know about an earlier one, by default each chat is a separate, blank transcript
Assuming a "memory" feature means the model learned something, it just saved a note and slips it into the transcript; the model still didn't change
Being surprised the model contradicts what it said an hour ago in a long chat, if that part fell out of the window, it's no longer in the transcript it sees
Not realizing a hidden system message is shaping every answer, the tool's built-in instructions are part of the conversation too
Not knowing whether memory is on, many apps switch it on by default, so check what it has saved and turn it off if you'd rather start clean each time
flags: "It doesn't remember my last chat", expected; each new conversation starts with an empty transcript unless a memory feature is on
"It suddenly forgot what we agreed earlier", in a long chat that part may have dropped out of the window, so it's no longer in the transcript
"The memory feature remembered something weird about me", that's a stored note you can usually view and delete in settings
"It behaves with a personality I didn't ask for", that's often the hidden system message the product added; a different tool will have a different one
ask: Am I expecting this chat to know something from a different conversation? If so, I need to bring it in, it won't carry over by itself.
Is this a fresh chat, or a long one where early details may have dropped off the transcript?
If I'm relying on a memory feature, do I actually know what it has stored about me?
Could a hidden system message be shaping these answers in a way I should account for?
Is this something I'd rather keep out of my history and memory? If so, would a temporary chat be the better choice?

MODULES.title: What Models Get Wrong
MODULES.tag: Hallucination and the knowledge cutoff, the two failure modes you must always expect
MODULES.why: A model that's right ninety percent of the time and confident one hundred percent of the time is genuinely dangerous if you don't know where the ten percent hides. This lesson names the two big, predictable ways models go wrong: they invent things that sound true (hallucination), and they don't know anything recent (the knowledge cutoff). These aren't rare glitches, they're built into how the engine works. Knowing exactly when to expect them is what separates someone who gets burned by AI from someone who uses it safely.
MODULES.mental: Both failures come straight from the one idea you already know: on its own, the model predicts likely-sounding text, it doesn't look anything up. So when it doesn't have a real answer, it often doesn't stop, it produces the most plausible-sounding text instead, and that invented-but-convincing answer is a hallucination. And because the model was trained once, in the past, its knowledge stops at a certain date, the knowledge cutoff, after which it knows nothing unless a tool feeds it fresh information. Picture a brilliant expert who's been locked in a room since some date in the past, and who, far too often, will smoothly make something up rather than say "I don't know". That single image tells you exactly when to be careful: anything recent, and anything where a confident guess would cost you.
concepts: Hallucination

When the model states something false as if it were true, a fake statistic, an invented quote, a citation to a paper that doesn't exist, a made-up feature. It happens because the model fills gaps with plausible text rather than admitting it doesn't know.
Why hallucination can't be fully switched off

It's the same machinery that makes the model useful: always producing likely-sounding text. Model makers have also found that training tends to reward a confident guess over an honest "I'm not sure", the way a multiple-choice test rewards guessing, and they're working to change that. You can reduce it (better prompts, giving it real sources, asking it to cite), but there's no setting that guarantees it never makes things up.
Knowledge cutoff

The date the model's training data stops. It knows nothing about events, prices, releases, or news after that point, and often isn't sure exactly where its own cutoff is. Ask about last week and it may confidently answer from an outdated world, or even insist that a real recent event never happened. Apps often tell it today's date, but knowing the date isn't the same as knowing the news.
Confidence is not a signal
The model sounds equally sure whether it's right, hallucinating, or answering from stale knowledge. You cannot tell from the tone, which is precisely why tone can't be your safety check.
It's worst on the specific and the obscure

Hallucination is most likely on precise, verifiable details (names, numbers, quotes, links, citations) about niche or recent topics, exactly the things that look most authoritative and are most tempting to copy.
Grounding reduces it

When you give the model the real source to work from, paste the document, or use a tool that searches, it has actual material to draw on instead of guessing. "Answer only from this text" is far safer than "answer from memory."
Search helps, but check the source

Many apps now search the web and show their sources, which cuts down on made-up facts. It doesn't make answers bulletproof: the model can misread a page, lean on a weak source, or attach a real link to a claim the page doesn't actually make. For anything that matters, click through and check the source says what the answer says.
mistakes: Trusting a confident answer on a recent topic, the model's knowledge stops at its cutoff and it won't reliably tell you it's out of date
Copying specific details (quotes, statistics, citations, links) without checking, these are exactly what hallucination produces most convincingly
Believing the model when it 'cites a source', it can invent realistic-looking sources that don't exist
Assuming a newer model, a thinking mode, or a web search means it's never wrong, each one lowers the odds, but none makes it immune
Asking it about today's news or live data and taking the answer at face value, without a search tool it literally cannot know
Trusting a cited answer without opening the source, the link can be real while the claim attached to it isn't
flags: "It gave me a source/quote/statistic", verify it exists before using it; fabricated-but-realistic references are a classic hallucination
"It told me about a recent event confidently", check whether that's even after its knowledge cutoff; it may be guessing from an old world
"It contradicted itself between answers", a sign it was generating plausible text rather than drawing on a stable fact
"It insisted it was right when I pushed back", confidence under pressure still isn't evidence; go check an actual source
"It agreed with me the moment I pushed back", caving isn't evidence either; models tend to tell you what you want to hear, so check a source rather than trusting the switch
"It told me that new thing doesn't exist", if it's newer than the model's knowledge cutoff, it may simply not know; check a current source
ask: Is this about something recent? If so, is it past the model's knowledge cutoff, and do I need a search tool or a real source instead?
Would being wrong here actually cost me, and if so, how will I verify it independently?
Did the model give me specific, copyable details (numbers, names, quotes, links)? Those are the ones to check first.
Could I make this safer by giving the model the real source to answer from, instead of asking it from memory?

MODULES.title: Beyond Text
MODULES.tag: Images, files, the internet, and tools, the extras bolted onto the text engine
MODULES.why: By now you know the core model only predicts text, and only knows what's in its training and your prompt. So how can ChatGPT look at a photo, read your PDF, search the web, run a calculation, talk with you out loud, or make a picture? The answer is that modern AI products bundle extra abilities around the text engine. Knowing which abilities are core to the model and which are bolt-on features explains what your particular tool can and can't do, and stops you from assuming every AI can do everything you've seen somewhere.
MODULES.mental: Think of the language model as a powerful engine, and the product you actually use (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) as a car built around that engine. The engine does text prediction (and some engines come with extra senses built in, like seeing images). Most of everything else, reading files, searching the internet, doing exact math, running code, is a capability the car adds on. Crucially, when the model needs something outside its own abilities, it doesn't magically gain a new power, it calls a tool: a separate piece of software that does the real work and hands the result back as text the model can use. So "can this AI do X?" almost always means "does this product give the model a tool for X?" Same engine, different cars, different features.
concepts: Multimodal (seeing and hearing)

Many models can now take in more than text, a photo, a screenshot, a chart, sometimes audio, and describe or reason about it. That's a genuine skill those models were trained to have, not something every model or app offers. It can still misread small print and numbers, so check anything precise.
Reading files

When you attach a PDF or document, the app turns it into something the model can take in and slips that into the prompt: the text pulled out of the file and, in some apps, pictures of each page too. The model isn't 'opening' the file, which is why a scan or a photo of a document can read fine in one app and draw a blank, or a garbled guess, in another.
Web search / browsing

By itself the model can't reach the internet. A search tool, when the product includes one, looks things up live and feeds the results into the prompt. That's how an AI can answer about today, it's reading fresh text the tool fetched, not 'knowing' it. Many apps now decide on their own when to search and list the sources they used, so you can tell when it happened.
Tools (the general idea)

A tool is any outside helper the model can call: a calculator, a search engine, a code runner, a database. The model decides it needs help, the tool does the exact work, and the result comes back as text. This is how AI gets reliable at things text-prediction is bad at.
Why tools make it more reliable

Letting a calculator do the math, or a search engine fetch the fact, replaces a shaky guess with an actual answer. Tools are how products patch over the model's weak spots, arithmetic, fresh info, exact lookups, without changing the engine itself.
Making pictures, video, and speech

When an AI makes a picture, a video clip, or a spoken reply, that's a different job from predicting text. Depending on the app, your request goes to a separate model built for images, video, or speech, or to a model trained to produce more than text. Either way it's another capability bundled into one friendly interface, with its own strengths and quirks.
Voice mode

Many apps let you talk and listen instead of typing. Some turn your speech into text, run the usual model, and read the answer aloud; others use models that work with audio directly, which is why they can reply faster and pick up on tone. Either way it's the same kind of assistant underneath, so it can be just as confidently wrong, only out loud.
AI inside everyday apps

AI now turns up inside tools you already use: summaries at the top of search results, writing helpers in email and documents, assistants on your phone. It's the same kind of engine with the same limits, so an AI summary in a search page or an inbox deserves the same quick check as any other AI answer.
mistakes: Assuming every AI can see images or search the web, most big chat apps can now, but plenty of AI features and apps can't, so check the one you're using
Thinking the model 'opened' your file the way you would, the app converted it first, and a scan or photo may come through garbled or not at all, depending on the app

MODULES.title: Putting It Together
MODULES.tag: Choosing a model and how hard it thinks, building cost intuition, and where to go next
MODULES.why: You now know what the engine is, how it reads, what it forgets, how to talk to it, where it fails, and what the extras do. This final lesson ties it into practical judgment: how to pick a model (and how hard it should think) for a task, a rough feel for what things cost, and a simple habit for deciding when to trust an answer. It's also your on-ramp, when you're ready to actually build things with these models, the Engineering Mastery course picks up right where this leaves off.
MODULES.mental: Everything in this course collapses into one working habit: match the model and your effort to what the task actually needs. A throwaway brainstorm doesn't need the biggest, priciest model or careful fact-checking. A client-facing claim or a medical question needs your best model, a tight prompt, real sources, and a human check. So before each task, ask two quick questions: how capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me? Cheap-and-fast for low stakes, careful-and-verified for high stakes. And when a problem is genuinely hard and multi-step, give the model room to think. You're not memorizing rules, you're learning to right-size your tool, which is exactly how a professional uses one.
concepts: Bigger model vs smaller model

Most providers offer a range: larger, smarter, slower, pricier models, and smaller, faster, cheaper ones. The big one isn't always the right call. For simple tasks the small one is quicker and far cheaper; save the heavyweight for genuinely hard work.
Fast mode vs thinking mode

Many apps also let you choose how hard the model thinks: a quick mode for everyday asks, and a "thinking" or higher-effort setting that works through the problem before answering. Thinking is slower and uses more of your budget or usage limits, so save it for multi-step problems like math, planning, tricky analysis, or code; it adds little to a quick rewrite or a simple question. Some apps decide for you automatically, which is a fine default.
A rough feel for cost

Cost tracks tokens, both what you send and what comes back. Short chats are nearly free; the expense comes from big pasted documents and long generated answers. You don't need exact numbers, just the instinct that 'huge input plus long output equals real money.' On a monthly app plan the same instinct applies to your usage limits: long chats, big files, the biggest models, and thinking modes use them up faster.
Match effort to stakes

Low-stakes, reversible task? Move fast, accept a good-enough answer. High-stakes or hard-to-undo? Use a stronger model, give it sources, and verify the output yourself. Right-sizing your caution is the core skill.
Know when to verify

Trust the model for drafting, brainstorming, explaining, and rephrasing. Verify it for facts, numbers, recent events, citations, and anything where being wrong has a cost. This single split prevents most AI mishaps.
Test it on what you already know

Before trusting a tool with a task you'll repeat, try it on a few examples where you already know the right answer. That five-minute check tells you more about how it handles your work than any leaderboard or ad.
Pick the tool with the right features

If you need current info, choose a product with web search. If you work with images or PDFs, choose one that handles them. The 'best' AI is the one whose bundled capabilities match what you're actually doing.
The app is doing a lot for you

Every time you chat, the product is quietly working on your behalf: re-sending the whole conversation, slipping in a hidden system message, and routing your words to a model someone else chose. Builders do all of that themselves by calling the model directly through an API, a way for their own software to hand text to the model and get text back. You don't need to write a line of code to finish here, but seeing the chat app as a convenient wrapper around a raw model call is exactly the shift the Engineering Mastery course starts from.
Where to go next

If you want to go from using these models to building with them, designing prompts at scale, wiring up tools, controlling cost in real systems, that's the Engineering Mastery course. Everything here is the foundation it assumes.

PLAIN.whatai: AI tools like ChatGPT are powered by something called a large language model. Underneath, it does one surprisingly simple thing: it predicts the next bit of text, again and again, until it has written a whole answer. On its own, it isn't looking things up, it has no real memory of you, and it doesn't "know" facts the way a person or a database does, it produces text that sounds right based on patterns it learned. That's why it can be incredibly helpful and also, sometimes, confidently wrong. This lesson is about that one core idea, because everything else in AI makes sense once you've got it.
PLAIN.tokens: Before an AI model can do anything with your text, it chops it into little pieces called tokens. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word, so common words are one piece and longer or unusual words get split into several. The model never sees letters or whole words the way you do, it sees this stream of tokens. That one fact quietly explains a lot: AI is priced by the token (both what you type and what it writes back), length limits are counted in tokens, and the model's odd weak spots, like miscounting the letters in a word, happen because it isn't looking at letters at all. You won't count tokens by hand, but knowing they exist makes AI's cost and quirks stop being mysterious.
PLAIN.context: An AI model has no memory of its own. Every time you send a message, it's handed one big block of text, the conversation so far plus your new message, and it can only look at what fits in that block. The size of that block is called the context window, and it's the model's short-term memory, like a desk with a hard edge. Whatever's on the desk, it can use; whatever falls off the edge when the conversation gets too long is simply gone (or, in some apps, boiled down to a short summary). That's why a model can 'forget' something you said much earlier, why pasting in a giant document can backfire, and why long chats slowly drift. The practical takeaway: you control what goes on the desk, and keeping it focused on what matters is the most useful AI skill there is.
PLAIN.prompting: A prompt is just the text you give an AI to work with, your question or instruction plus any context you include. The model takes it literally and can't read your mind, so the quality of your prompt drives the quality of the answer. The trick isn't secret phrases, it's treating the model like a brilliant new assistant on their first day: tell it clearly what you want done, give it the background it needs, and say what a good answer looks like (a list, a short paragraph, a friendly tone, a certain length). If the first reply is close but not quite right, just tell it what to change, prompting is a back-and-forth, not a one-shot spell. Vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out. This is the single highest-leverage skill in the whole course.
PLAIN.chat: Chatting with an AI feels like talking to someone who remembers the conversation, but the model itself remembers nothing between messages, it's what engineers call stateless. The continuity is an illusion created by the chat app: every time you hit send, the app re-sends the entire conversation so far, your messages and the model's replies, all glued together, plus your new message. The model reads that whole transcript, answers, and forgets again. That's why a brand-new chat starts blank (empty transcript), why 'memory' features (often on by default now) are a separate add-on that saves notes and slips them into the transcript, and why a hidden 'system message' the product adds at the top can quietly shape every answer. Once you see that the memory lives in the re-sent transcript and not in the model, chat tools stop being mysterious.
PLAIN.limits: Models go wrong in two big, predictable ways, and both come from the same fact: the model predicts plausible-sounding text, it doesn't look things up. First, when it doesn't actually know something, it tends to make up a convincing answer rather than admit it, fake statistics, invented quotes, citations to papers that don't exist. That's called hallucination, and there's no setting that fully turns it off. Second, the model was trained once in the past, so its knowledge stops at a certain date, the knowledge cutoff, and it knows nothing newer unless a tool feeds it fresh information. Picture a brilliant expert locked in a room since some point in the past, who too often smoothly invents an answer instead of saying 'I don't know.' The danger is that it sounds just as confident when it's wrong, so confidence is never your safety check. Be especially careful with specific details and anything recent, and verify anything where being wrong would cost you. Answers that come with sources are safer, but open the source when it matters.
PLAIN.tools: The core AI model only predicts text, so how can your app look at a photo, read your PDF, search the web, talk out loud, or do math? Modern AI products bundle extra abilities around the text engine. Think of the model as an engine and the product (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) as a car built around it: reading files, searching the internet, running calculations, voice, making pictures, these are features the car adds (and some engines come with built-in senses, like seeing images). When the model needs something outside its own ability, it calls a tool, a separate piece of software that does the real work and hands the result back as text. Reading a file means the app converted it first; searching the web means a tool fetched fresh pages; getting the math right means a calculator did it. So 'can this AI do X?' really means 'does this product give the model a tool for X?' Same engine, different cars, different features, which is why two AI apps can have very different abilities.
PLAIN.using: This lesson ties everything together into a single working habit: match the model, and your own effort, to what the task actually needs. Providers offer bigger, smarter, slower, pricier models and smaller, faster, cheaper ones, and the big one isn't always right, save it for genuinely hard work. Many apps also offer a 'thinking' mode: slower and heavier on your limits, but worth it for hard, multi-step problems. Cost tracks tokens, so short chats are nearly free and the expense comes from big pasted documents and long answers; you just need the instinct that 'huge input plus long output equals real money' (on a monthly plan, the same things eat into your usage limits). Before each task, ask two questions: how capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me? Move fast and accept good-enough for low-stakes work; use a stronger model, give it real sources, and verify the output for anything high-stakes. Trust it for drafting, brainstorming, and rephrasing; verify it for facts, numbers, recent events, and citations. That's how a professional uses the tool, and if you're ready to go from using these models to building with them, the Engineering Mastery course picks up right here.

GLOSSARY: A broad term for software that does things we used to think required human intelligence, like understanding language or recognizing images. Today, most of the "AI" people talk about is built on large language models.

The engine behind tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. A program trained on a huge amount of text whose core skill is predicting the next word, which turns out to be enough to write, answer, and reason.
Short for the AI program itself, the trained "brain" you send text to and get text back from. "The model" and "the LLM" usually mean the same thing.
The basic move an LLM makes: given the text so far, guess the most likely next chunk. Repeat that thousands of times and you get a full answer.

The process, finished before you ever use the model, of showing it enormous amounts of text so it gets good at predicting it, followed by fine-tuning to make it a helpful assistant. Chatting with it afterward doesn't change it.

Extra training on a narrower set of examples, such as sample conversations, human ratings, and practice problems with checkable answers, that shapes how a model behaves. It's how a raw text-predictor becomes a helpful assistant, and it happens before you use the model, not while you chat.
To produce new text on the spot, rather than look it up. LLMs generate answers, which is why they can be both creative and occasionally wrong.

A setting, or a kind of model, where the AI writes out working notes before answering: breaking the problem down, trying an approach, checking it. Slower and uses more tokens, but better on hard, multi-step problems. It's still text prediction, not a mind.
Popular chat products, each built on top of a large language model. The differences you notice are mostly in the product wrapped around the model, not a different kind of engine.
The small chunk of text a model actually reads and writes, often a common word, a word-piece, or a punctuation mark. As a rough rule, one token is about four characters, or three-quarters of a word.
Slicing your text into tokens before the model sees it. It happens automatically every time, for both your input and the model's output.
Input tokens are everything you send in (your prompt plus any pasted text); output tokens are everything the model writes back. Both are counted, and both affect speed and cost.
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, a model can look at in one go. It must hold the whole conversation, your message, any pasted files, and the answer being written, all at once.
A plain-English name for what's in the context window right now: the only thing the model can actually use this turn. It doesn't remember anything outside that window by default.

What happens when a conversation grows past the window: the earliest messages stop being included (or get boiled down to a summary), so the model can no longer refer to them in full, it's not choosing to forget, it simply can't see them.

What some apps do when you give them more material than fits in the window: search it and put only the most relevant pieces in front of the model for each question. Handy for big projects, but the model can miss anything that wasn't pulled in.
The text you give the model to work with: your question or instruction plus any context or examples. It's the entire input the model has, so anything you leave out, it doesn't know.
The skill of writing clear instructions for a model. Less about clever tricks, more about saying plainly what you want, giving the needed context, and describing what a good answer looks like.

Refining your request after seeing the first answer, telling the model what to change ('shorter', 'more formal', 'focus on this') instead of rewriting from scratch. Prompting is a back-and-forth, not one shot.
Describes the model keeping no memory between turns: each message is handled on its own, as if it were the first. Any sense of an ongoing conversation comes from outside the model.
The running transcript of everything said so far, your messages and the model's replies. The chat app stores it and re-sends the whole thing each turn so the model has the full picture.

A hidden instruction most chat tools add at the very top of the transcript, before your first word, telling the model how to behave. You don't see it, but it shapes the tone and rules of every answer.

An extra built on top of the model, often switched on by default, that saves notes about you (or draws on past chats) and slips them into the transcript automatically. The model didn't 'learn', the app just stores and re-inserts the notes; you can usually view, edit, or turn them off.

A standing brief you write once, about yourself, your preferences, or a project (sometimes with files attached), that the app adds to every chat in that space. Like a system message you control; the model still isn't remembering anything.
A chat that isn't saved to your history, doesn't feed the memory feature, and isn't used to train future models. The company may still keep it briefly for safety checks.

When a model states something false as if it were true, a fake quote, an invented statistic, a citation to a paper that doesn't exist. It happens because the model fills gaps with plausible text instead of admitting it doesn't know.

The date a model's training data stops. It knows nothing about events, prices, or releases after that point, and often isn't sure exactly when its own cutoff is, so it may answer recent questions from an outdated world.
Giving the model real material to answer from, a pasted document or a tool's search results, instead of asking it from memory. Grounded answers are far less likely to be made up.
Describes a model that can work with more than text, taking in images or audio and, for some, producing pictures or speech too. It's a capability of specific models, not a universal power.

Any outside helper a model can call when it needs something beyond text prediction: a calculator, a web search, a code runner, a database. The tool does the real work and hands the result back as text the model can use.

A tool that lets an AI product look things up live on the internet and feed the results into the prompt. The core model can't reach the web by itself; many apps now search automatically and show their sources, but not every product has it.

A way to talk with an AI app and hear it answer. Some versions turn your speech into text and back; others use models that handle audio directly. It's the same kind of assistant underneath, with the same limits.
On a monthly app plan, the cap on how much you can use the AI in a given period. Long chats, big files, the biggest models, and thinking modes tend to use it up faster.

whatai.worked: Ask a model, "What's the capital of France?" and it answers "Paris", instantly and correctly. It feels like it looked that up in a database. It didn't. The phrase "the capital of France is" appeared so many times in its training text, always followed by "Paris", that "Paris" is overwhelmingly the most likely next word. The model is just completing the pattern. Now ask it something obscure that only sounds answerable, like the exact words a minor local politician used in a speech decades ago. If that speech barely appeared in its training text, the most likely-looking continuation is still a quote-shaped sentence, so it may cheerfully invent a plausible one. (Newer models have learned to say "I don't know" to obviously unknowable questions, like what you ate last Tuesday; it's the obscure-but-answerable kind that still trips them up.) Same engine, same behavior, completing text. The difference is that one pattern was all over its training data and the other one it had to make up. Holding both examples in your head at once is the whole lesson: right answers and made-up answers come out of the exact same machine, the same way.
good: You treat the model as a confident draft-writer, not a source of truth
You double-check anything where being wrong would actually cost you
You're not surprised when it makes something up, you expect it and verify
You reach for a real search or a document when you need current or private facts
You ask it to generate, brainstorm, rephrase, and explain, where it genuinely shines
whatai.build: Try this five-minute experiment in any chat AI. First, ask it a well-known fact ("What year did the first iPhone come out?"), it will likely nail it. Then ask it, without letting it search the web, for something specific and obscure that sounds answerable, like the exact wording of a minor rule in a little-known board game, or a quote from a small-town newspaper story. See whether it admits it isn't sure, or hands you a confident, specific answer you can't find anywhere when you check. Seeing the same tool be reliably right and, sometimes, confidently wrong, back to back, makes the "text-prediction machine" idea stick far better than any explanation.

tokens.worked: Take the simple sentence "I love tokenization!" To you, that's three words. To the model, it might be five tokens: "I", " love" (the space rides along), " token", "ization", and "!". Notice three things. First, the common word "love" is a single token, but the longer, less common word "tokenization" got split into pieces. Second, spaces and punctuation are tokens too. Third, and this is the punchline, the model never saw the letters t-o-k-e-n; it saw the chunks " token" and "ization". So if you ask it, "how many letter z's are in that sentence?", it has to reason about something it can't actually see, and it often gets it wrong. The same blindness that makes it stumble on counting letters is exactly why it can read almost any text, in any language, including words it was never trained on: it just spells the unfamiliar word out of smaller, familiar tokens.
good: You think in rough tokens, not exact words, when you estimate length or cost (a chunky paragraph is a few hundred tokens, not a precise figure)
You remember that pasted text counts as input tokens, so you trim documents down to the part that matters
You don't ask the model to do letter-level tasks (counting characters, exact anagrams) and trust the result, you reach for a real tool
You're not surprised that a long answer costs more than a short one, output tokens are billed too
You notice that the same content can cost more in some languages, and factor that in if it matters
tokens.build: Spend five minutes with a free online tokenizer (search "OpenAI tokenizer" or "Tiktokenizer" and open the visual one). Paste in a normal sentence and watch it split into colored chunks, count them. Then paste a made-up word like "flibbertigibbeting" and see it shatter into many tiny pieces. Finally, paste the same sentence translated into another language and compare the token count. In five minutes you'll have seen, with your own eyes, why common words are cheap, rare words are expensive, and the model reads in chunks rather than letters.

context.worked: Imagine a long chat with an assistant. Near the start, you mention, "My dog's name is Pixel." You then talk for forty more messages about a totally different project, pasting in several long documents along the way. Finally you ask, "What's my dog's name?" and the model says it doesn't know, or worse, confidently guesses "Max." It didn't betray you. As the conversation grew, it eventually got longer than the context window, and the earliest messages, including the one about Pixel, slid off the edge (or, in an app that summarizes old messages, got boiled down to a summary that never mentioned the dog). From the model's point of view in that final turn, you simply never mentioned a dog. The model isn't remembering and then forgetting; each turn it only ever sees what currently fits in the window. Now flip it around: if instead you'd said, "Earlier I told you my dog's name, remind me to use it, his name is Pixel," right before asking, the detail would be back on the desk and the model would nail it. Same model, same question, completely different result, because of what was in the window at the moment you asked.
good: You restate key details when a conversation has gotten long, rather than assuming the model still has them
You paste in only the relevant part of a document, not the whole thing, so the important bit isn't buried
You start a fresh chat (with a short summary) when an old one has drifted, instead of fighting the drift
You keep one task per conversation when accuracy matters, so unrelated context doesn't confuse things
You put your actual question where it's easy to find, not buried under a wall of pasted text
context.build: Run a two-part experiment in any chat AI. Part one: in a brand-new chat, tell it a specific made-up fact about yourself in the first message ("My favorite number is 17"), then paste in something long and unrelated, a few pages of any article, and have a short back-and-forth about it. Now ask, "What's my favorite number?" With today's big windows it will probably still know, and that's the point: the fact is still on the desk. Part two: open a second brand-new chat (a temporary or incognito one, so no memory feature helps out) and ask the same question. It can't know, because this desk started empty. Now type the fact and ask again: instant recall. Seeing the same model know, not know, and know again, decided entirely by what was on the desk when you asked, turns 'the context window' from an abstract phrase into something you can feel.

prompting.worked: Watch one prompt improve in three steps. Step one, the vague version: "Write about our coffee shop." The model has nothing to go on, so it produces something generic that could describe any cafe anywhere. Step two, add the task and audience: "Write a short, warm welcome blurb for the About page of our neighborhood coffee shop, aimed at first-time visitors." Already far better, it now knows what, for whom, and the tone. Step three, add the shape and a detail: "...in three sentences, friendly but not cutesy, and mention that we roast our own beans." Now you'll get something you could almost paste straight in. Nothing clever happened, no magic words, you just told a capable assistant what you actually wanted. And if the result is still a touch off, you don't start over: you say "good, but make the first sentence punchier." That last move, refining instead of rewriting, is the habit that makes prompting feel easy.
good: You state the task plainly, what you want done, not just the topic
You include the context the model couldn't otherwise know (audience, goal, relevant background)
You say what a good answer looks like, format, length, and tone
You paste an example when you have one, and say 'like this'
You refine in small steps when the first answer is close, instead of starting from scratch
prompting.build: Pick any real task you'd actually use AI for, an email, a summary, a list of ideas. Write the laziest one-line prompt for it and note the answer. Then rewrite the prompt with three additions: the specific task, the context (who it's for, what it's about), and the format you want. Send it again and compare. Finally, take that second answer and refine it once with a single instruction ('shorter', 'warmer', 'add a call to action'). In five minutes you'll have felt the whole arc, vague to specific to refined, on a task you care about, which is the fastest way to make prompting a habit instead of a theory.

chat.worked: Here's the illusion taken apart. You open a chat and type "My name is Sam." The model replies, "Nice to meet you, Sam." Next you ask, "What's my name?" and it says "Sam." It feels like it remembered. But watch what the app actually sent on that second turn: not just "What's my name?", but the entire transcript, "My name is Sam." / "Nice to meet you, Sam." / "What's my name?", all glued together and handed over fresh. The model read the whole thing top to bottom and saw your name sitting right there in the text. It didn't recall anything; it re-read a transcript that happened to contain the answer. Now picture the same setup but a thousand messages long, until that first "My name is Sam" finally falls out of the context window. Ask "What's my name?" again and the model can't tell you, the line is no longer in the transcript it receives. Same model, same question, different answer, entirely because of what's in the re-sent transcript. The memory was never in the model; it was in the text being re-handed to it each turn.

limits.worked: Ask a model, telling it not to search the web, "Give me three peer-reviewed studies showing that houseplants improve office productivity, with authors and years." You'll likely get exactly that: three crisp citations, real-sounding author names, plausible journals, recent years. It looks authoritative. Now try to find one of them, search the title, the authors. There's a good chance one or more simply does not exist. The model wasn't lying or broken; you asked for the shape of an answer (citations) on a specific topic, and it produced the most likely-looking text of that shape, inventing the details it didn't actually have. That's hallucination in its most dangerous form, because the polish makes it feel trustworthy. Let the app search first and the citations are much more likely to be real, but open them anyway: a genuine study attached to a claim it doesn't actually make is the newer version of the same trap. Now stack the second failure on top: ask it, with search off, "What major news happened last week?" and it may answer confidently about events, except its training stopped months or years ago, so it's describing a world that's out of date, with no built-in way to tell you so. One engine, two predictable failures, made-up specifics and stale knowledge, both wearing the same confident voice. Spotting them is the whole skill.

tools.worked: Picture asking an AI, "What's 4,817 times 9,231, and what's the weather in Lisbon right now?" A plain text model, on its own, would have to predict its way through the multiplication (big multiplications are exactly where it can land close but wrong) and would have no idea about today's weather, its knowledge is frozen and it can't see outside. But in a modern product, something smarter happens. For the math, the model recognizes it needs help and calls a calculator tool: the calculator does the exact arithmetic and hands back the real number, which the model drops into its answer. For the weather, it calls a search tool that fetches the current conditions and feeds that fresh text into the prompt, now the model can report it accurately (in many apps you'll even see a note that it searched, with links to its sources). Notice what changed: the engine didn't suddenly get good at math or gain a window to the world. The product routed each sub-task to a tool built for it, and the model stitched the results into one fluent reply. That's the entire pattern behind 'AI that can do anything', it's a text engine surrounded by helpers it knows how to call.

using.worked: Let's run two real tasks through the habit and watch the right choice fall out. Task one: brainstorm ten playful names for a houseplant shop. Stakes are low, it's reversible, and it's pure creative generation, the model's home turf. So: reach for a smaller, faster, cheaper model or a quick mode, write a quick prompt, and happily accept a good-enough list. No fact-checking needed, no heavyweight model, no fuss. Task two: draft a paragraph for a patient handout about a medication's side effects. Completely different. Being wrong here could hurt someone, so the stakes are high and the facts must be exact. That's the whole course, distilled into a habit you can run in five seconds before any task.

whatai.mech:
Here's a little more of what's happening under the hood, no math required. When you send the model text, it first chops it into small chunks (you'll meet these as tokens in the next lesson). Then it runs those chunks through a giant web of numbers, learned during training, that has effectively absorbed the statistical patterns of how language tends to flow. The output of all that is a ranked list of likely next chunks, with a probability on each. The model picks one, adds it to the text, and runs the whole process again for the next chunk. It repeats this until it decides the answer is complete.

Two things follow from this, and they explain almost everything beginners find confusing. First, the model has no separate store of facts to check against. "Knowing" that Paris is the capital of France just means that, given the surrounding words, "Paris" comes out on top. When a fact was rare or absent in training, the most likely next words can be plausible-sounding nonsense, that's a hallucination, and it isn't a bug that gets patched away. Second, the model is frozen. Training happened once, in the past, so it has a knowledge cutoff and knows nothing about you or about events after that date, unless a product feature explicitly feeds it that information at the moment you ask.

One more piece is worth knowing now, because apps advertise it: some models can "think" before they answer. That's the same loop with an extra step at the front: the model first writes out working notes (restating the problem, trying an approach, checking it) and then writes the answer, steered by its own notes. It helps a lot on multi-step problems and costs extra time and tokens. And the notes you can sometimes peek at are usually a summary, not a guaranteed record of how the model really reached its answer.
trade: The same skill that lets it write and brainstorm freely is what lets it confidently make facts up
Fluency is the model's whole goal; it is not a signal that the answer is right
By itself the model can't know today's news or your private data; that needs an extra step, like search or pasting it in
scale: Helpful framing for everyday use, not engineering, since this is a foundations course: the bigger and more capable the model, the slower and more expensive each answer tends to be, so you don't need the biggest model for simple tasks
The same question can cost more or less depending on how long your input and the answer are, you'll see exactly why in the next lesson on tokens
If a tool feels slow, it's often the model writing a long answer one chunk at a time (or thinking before it answers), asking for a shorter answer genuinely makes it faster

whatai.interview: Here's how I'd explain it to a friend in two sentences. A large language model is a text-prediction machine: you give it words, and it keeps guessing the most likely next word until it has written a full answer, like an incredibly well-read autocomplete. It isn't looking anything up and it doesn't truly know facts, which is why it can be amazingly helpful and also, sometimes, confidently and completely wrong.

tokens.mech:
A little more under the hood, still no math. Every model ships with a fixed vocabulary of tokens, often a hundred thousand or more, built once when the model was made. The pieces aren't chosen by hand; a process scans huge amounts of text and keeps the chunks that show up most often. Very common words earn their own single token. Rarer words get assembled from smaller pieces, and truly unusual strings (a random password, a long chemical name) can break down almost letter by letter. That's the trade that makes the whole thing work: a manageable, fixed set of pieces that can still spell out absolutely anything.

This is why the model's view of text is genuinely different from yours, and it explains the quirks. It sees " token" + "ization", not t-o-k-e-n-i-z-a-t-i-o-n, so counting letters, reversing a word, or perfect spelling are awkward, the raw letters aren't really visible to it. It also explains cost and limits: since everything is measured in tokens, your bill and your length limit both track token counts, and languages that happen to split into more tokens cost more to process for the very same meaning. None of this is a flaw to be fixed; it's just the shape of how the model reads.
trade: Everyday words are cheap and quick; long, rare, or made-up words cost more tokens and a bit more processing
Lets it handle any text including unseen words, but makes letter-level tasks (counting, spelling, reversing) genuinely shaky
Fewer tokens is cheaper and faster; the skill is including what matters and trimming what doesn't
scale: Rough rule of thumb for everyday estimating: about seven hundred fifty words is around a thousand tokens, so a few pages of text is several thousand tokens (some newer models count noticeably more tokens for the same text)
Both halves count toward cost: the text you send (input) and the text the model writes back (output), and the answer is often the bigger, pricier half
On a monthly app plan you won't see a per-token bill, but the same things, long chats, big files, the biggest models, and thinking modes, tend to use up your usage limits faster
If a long answer feels slow, it's the model emitting tokens one at a time, asking for a shorter or more focused answer genuinely speeds things up and lowers cost
sec: Remember the text you paste is sent to the company running the model and counts as tokens, so don't paste secrets or other people's private data just to save yourself some typing
For any letter-perfect task (a license key, an exact code, a precise count of characters), don't trust the model's token's-eye view, double-check with a tool that actually sees the characters
If a vendor charges by tokens, a surprise bill usually traces back to large pasted inputs, very long outputs, or lots of hidden thinking, watch all three
tokens.interview: Here's the friend-explanation. Before an AI model reads your text, it chops it into little chunks called tokens, roughly three-quarters of a word each, so common words are one chunk and rare ones get split up. The model only ever sees those chunks, never the individual letters. That single fact explains three things at once: you're billed by the token for both what you type and what it writes, length limits are counted in tokens, and the model fumbles letter-level tasks like counting characters because it genuinely isn't looking at letters.

context.mech:
Here's what's really happening when you 'have a conversation' with an AI, and it surprises almost everyone. The model has no memory between turns. Each time you press send, the app quietly glues together the entire conversation so far, every earlier message from both of you, plus any files you attached and your new question, into one long block of text, and hands that whole block to the model fresh. The model reads it, predicts an answer, and then forgets it ever happened. The illusion of an ongoing chat is really the app re-sending the whole history every single time.

That block has a maximum size, the context window, measured in tokens. As long as the conversation fits, everything works and the model appears to 'remember.' But when the history grows past the window, something has to give: depending on the app, the oldest messages are dropped, or condensed into a short summary, so the rest still fits (some apps simply ask you to start a new chat). Whatever was dropped, or boiled down, is simply not in the block the model receives in full, so it cannot use those details, it's not forgetting, it never saw them this turn. Two practical consequences follow. First, bigger windows help but never make the limit vanish, and a fuller window is slower and costs more. Second, more text is not automatically better: when the window is crammed with marginally-relevant stuff, the one detail that matters is easy to miss, which is why a focused context usually beats a giant one.
trade: Long chats drift as early context drops off; starting fresh with a short summary often restores accuracy
Paste everything vs paste the relevant part
A giant paste can bury the key detail and dilute the answer; a focused excerpt usually performs better
More room lets you include more, but every extra token in the window is slower and more expensive, and can add noise
scale: Context windows are advertised per model, often large enough for hundreds of pages and sometimes several whole books, but the limit is still real and still counted in tokens
A fuller window costs more and responds slower, because everything in it has to be processed every single turn, so don't fill it just because you can
If a chat is getting expensive or sluggish, it's often because the growing history is being re-sent each turn, summarizing and starting fresh resets that
sec: Everything in the window is something the model will read and may act on, so be careful pasting in text from untrusted sources, hidden instructions inside it can sway the answer
Don't leave sensitive details sitting in a long shared conversation longer than needed; what's in the window is what gets sent each turn
When precision matters, confirm the specific fact you care about is actually still in the conversation (not fallen off the edge) before you rely on the model's answer
context.interview: The friend-version goes like this. An AI model has no memory of its own, so every time you send a message, the app hands it the whole conversation so far plus your new message as one big block of text, and the model only sees what's in that block. The block has a size limit called the context window; when the chat grows past it, the oldest messages drop off (or get squeezed into a summary) and the model genuinely can't see them in full anymore. That's why it 'forgets' early details and why cramming in a huge document can backfire, the fix is to keep the window focused on what actually matters.

prompting.mech:
A little more on why phrasing matters so much, and it connects straight back to lesson one. The model predicts the next chunk of text based on everything in the prompt so far. Your prompt isn't a command that flips a switch; it's the starting text that steers every prediction that follows. A vague opening ("write about dogs") leaves the most-likely continuation wide open, so the model drifts toward the bland, average, could-be-anything answer, because that's statistically the safe path. A specific opening ("write a three-sentence, upbeat intro for a dog-walking flyer aimed at busy professionals") narrows the likely continuations dramatically, so the answer lands much closer to what you pictured.

This is also why examples are so powerful. When you paste a sample and say "like this," you've put a concrete pattern right into the text the model is continuing, and continuing a pattern is exactly what it's best at. And it's why iterating works: when you reply "shorter, and warmer," that feedback becomes part of the running prompt, so the next prediction is steered by it. You're not arguing with a person, you're adjusting the text that shapes the next guess. Seen this way, good prompting isn't a bag of tricks, it's just giving the prediction engine a clear, well-pointed starting line.
trade: A quick vague ask is less typing but gets a generic answer; a specific ask takes a moment longer and usually nails it
One big prompt vs step by step
Cramming every requirement in at once can lose one; breaking a complex task into steps is often more reliable
Describing the format works, but pasting one good example of it often teaches the model faster and more precisely
scale: A longer, more detailed prompt costs a few more tokens, this is almost always worth it, since a good answer the first time beats several cheap, useless ones
Iterating (a few short follow-ups) is cheap and fast, you don't have to get the perfect prompt on the first try, refining is a normal part of the flow
If you reuse a prompt often, it's worth polishing once and saving it; a good saved prompt pays for itself every time you use it
sec: Only include the context the task needs, don't paste private or sensitive details into a prompt just to be thorough, remember it's sent to the company running the model
Be specific about what you don't want too ("don't make up statistics," "only use the text I gave you"), it meaningfully reduces invented content
