prompting.interview: Here's the friend-explanation. A prompt is just the text you give the model, and it takes it completely literally, it can't read your mind or see anything you haven't shared, so the clearer your instructions, the better the answer. Treat it like briefing a sharp new assistant on day one: say what you want done, give the context they'd need, and describe what a good result looks like, a list, a short paragraph, a friendly tone. And if the first reply is close but not quite right, you don't start over, you just tell it what to change. Prompting is a back-and-forth, not a magic phrase.

chat.mech:
Let's make the illusion fully concrete, because once you see it you can't unsee it. The model is a function that takes a block of text in and gives a block of text out, with nothing remembered in between. A chat app turns that memoryless function into a flowing conversation with one trick: it keeps a transcript. Every turn, it does the same four things, appends your new message to the transcript, glues the whole transcript into one text block (usually with a hidden system message pinned at the very top, setting the assistant's behavior), sends that entire block to the model, and appends the reply back onto the transcript. Repeat. The model never sees a 'conversation', it sees one long document, freshly handed over each turn.

Three real consequences fall out of this. First, a new chat is a new transcript, empty except for the system message (and any memory notes the app adds), which is why it knows nothing else about your other chats. Second, this is where the context window from lesson three bites: as the transcript grows past the window, the oldest lines get trimmed to fit, so 'it forgot' is really 'that line is no longer in the document it received.' Third, a memory feature is just an extra step that, before sending, looks up saved notes about you (or relevant bits of your past chats) and quietly inserts them into the transcript, the model still didn't learn anything, the app just put the note in front of it. Custom instructions and projects work the same way: text you wrote once, re-inserted every turn. The whole magic of chat is bookkeeping around a function with no memory.
trade: A memoryless model is simpler and more predictable; the app re-sending the transcript is what creates the feeling of memory
No memory feature vs memory on
Off means every chat starts clean (more private, more repetitive); on means it recalls saved notes (handier, but stores things about you)
Long single chat vs fresh chats
One long chat keeps everything until it overflows the window; starting fresh keeps things clean but you re-supply what matters
Regular chats are saved and can feed memory; temporary chats aren't saved or remembered, but you lose the history and must re-supply any context
scale: Because the whole transcript is re-sent every turn, a long conversation gets more expensive and slower with each message, it's not just your latest question being processed, it's everything before it too
Starting a fresh chat with a short summary resets that cost, you carry forward only what matters instead of dragging the entire history
Memory features and hidden system messages add a little to every prompt, usually small, but it's text that gets sent each turn alongside your own
sec: What's in the transcript is what gets sent each turn, so don't leave passwords or sensitive personal details sitting in a long conversation longer than you need them
If a memory feature is on, periodically check what it has saved about you, it's inserting those notes into your chats, and you can usually view, edit, or clear them
Be cautious pasting text from untrusted sources into a chat, hidden instructions buried in it become part of the transcript the model reads and may sway its replies
A temporary or incognito chat keeps a conversation out of your history and memory, but the company may still hold it briefly for safety checks, so treat it as a privacy step, not a vanishing act
chat.interview: The friend-version: when you chat with an AI, it feels like it's remembering the conversation, but the model itself remembers nothing between messages, it's what's called stateless. The trick is that the chat app re-sends the entire conversation so far, every message from both of you, plus a hidden instruction at the top, as one big block of text every single turn. The model reads that whole transcript, replies, and forgets again. So the 'memory' isn't in the model, it's in the transcript the app keeps re-handing it, which is exactly why a brand-new chat starts blank, apart from any memory notes the app slips in.

limits.mech:
Both failures trace back to one line from lesson one: the model outputs the most likely next text, it has no separate store of facts to check against. So picture the model reaching a point where the honest answer is 'I don't actually know.' Nothing in the machinery reliably produces that pause: "I'm not sure" is just one more possible output, and model makers have found that training often rewards a confident guess over an honest "I don't know", much as a multiple-choice test rewards guessing. So it emits the most plausible continuation, and a confident, specific-sounding answer is often more 'answer-shaped' than a hedge, so out comes a fluent fabrication. That's a hallucination: not a lie, not a bug, just the prediction engine doing its only job where it lacks real material. This is why it's worst on precise, obscure details, there the gap between 'sounds right' and 'is right' is widest, and why grounding (handing it the real source) helps so much: now the likely-next-text is anchored to actual material instead of thin air. Web search is grounding done for you, which is why answers with sources are usually more reliable, though the model can still misread a page or cite one that doesn't say what it claims.

The knowledge cutoff is the second failure and it's even simpler. Training happened once, ending on some date. Everything after that, last week's news, this year's prices, the newest release, was never in the data, so the patterns simply aren't there. Worse, the model usually can't reliably report its own cutoff or notice that your question is about 'after' it, so it answers from its frozen worldview with the same confidence as everything else. Put the two together and you get the rule that protects you: be most careful exactly when an answer is most specific or most recent, because that's where confident and correct are most likely to come apart.
trade: The drive to always produce an answer is what makes it useful and what makes it hallucinate; it doesn't reliably say 'I don't know'
By itself it's stuck at its cutoff; a search tool can fetch fresh info, but only if the product has one and it actually runs
Answer from memory vs from a source
Asking from memory is easy but guess-prone; pasting the real source ('use only this') trades a little effort for far fewer made-up facts
A link next to a claim feels like proof; only opening it and finding the claim there actually is
scale: Newer, stronger models tend to hallucinate less and have more recent cutoffs, and thinking modes and web search help too, but 'less' is not 'never', so the verify-the-important-stuff habit applies to every model and every mode
Grounding the model in a pasted source or a search result usually costs more tokens (you're sending more text), and it's almost always worth it when accuracy matters
Asking the model to show its reasoning or cite where a claim came from costs a little more output but makes it far easier for you to catch a fabrication
sec: Never let a model be the last word on anything safety-critical, medical, legal, financial, or where someone could be harmed, use it to get oriented, then confirm with a qualified human or an authoritative source
Treat any specific quote, statistic, citation, or link as unverified until you've checked it exists, realistic-looking fabricated references are the most common and most damaging hallucination
For recent or time-sensitive questions, assume the model may be out of date unless you can confirm a search tool actually ran and pulled current information
limits.interview: Here's how I'd put it to a friend. AI models fail in two predictable ways, and both come from the fact that they predict likely text instead of looking things up. First, when a model doesn't really know something, it tends to invent a convincing answer rather than admit it, fake quotes, made-up statistics, citations to papers that don't exist, that's called hallucination, and there's no setting that fully turns it off. Second, it was trained once in the past, so its knowledge stops at a cutoff date and it knows nothing newer. Picture a brilliant expert locked in a room since some point in the past, who too often smoothly makes something up instead of saying 'I don't know.' The catch is it sounds just as confident when it's wrong, so always double-check anything specific or recent, and when it shows sources, open the ones that matter.

tools.mech:
Here's the mechanism behind 'AI that can do anything', and it's tidier than it looks. The text model stays exactly what you learned: a next-text predictor that knows only its training and the current prompt. Tools are separate programs the product makes available, a calculator, a web search, a file reader, a code runner, an image generator. The clever part is that the model can be trained to recognize when a task is beyond it and to emit a little request like 'search for X' or 'calculate Y' instead of guessing. The surrounding product spots that request, runs the real tool, and pastes the tool's result back into the prompt as fresh text. Then the model continues, now with a real answer to work from. From your seat it looks like one smart assistant; under the hood it's a text engine orchestrating helpers.

This reframes the whole question of 'what can this AI do?' It's not about the engine, which is the same text predictor everywhere, it's about which tools the product wired up. Image input ('multimodal') is a genuine model capability some models have and others don't. Reading a PDF means the app extracts the text and, in some apps, also shows the model a picture of each page, which is why a scan can work in one app and defeat another. Answering about today is a search tool fetching pages, which is why, with no such tool, the model is stuck at its cutoff. Even 'drawing a picture', making a video clip, or answering out loud is the product handing your request to a model built or trained for that job, sometimes a separate model entirely. Same friendly chat box, very different machinery behind each button, and knowing which is which tells you exactly what to expect.
trade: Model alone vs model plus tools
The bare model only predicts text; tools add real abilities (math, search, files) but each is a feature the product had to build in
Search gives fresh answers but only when it actually runs; trained-in knowledge is instant but stuck at the cutoff
Convenience of one app vs right capabilities
One tool that does everything is convenient, but the better choice is the product whose specific features match what you actually need
Voice is quick and hands-free; text is easier to skim, check, and copy, so switch to text for anything you need to verify
scale: Tools add steps, a web search or file read happens before the model can answer, so tool-using replies are often a bit slower than plain text ones
Feeding a tool's results (search snippets, extracted file text) into the prompt adds tokens, so capable, tool-rich answers can cost more than a quick text-only reply
For exact work, math, data lookups, the right move is letting a tool do it; the small extra cost buys a correct answer instead of a confident guess
sec: When a tool reads your files or a search pulls in outside pages, that content enters the prompt, be aware that pasted or fetched text from untrusted sources can carry hidden instructions
Don't assume an answer is current just because the product can search; confirm a search actually ran (look for a source or link) before trusting fresh-sounding claims
Files you upload are processed by the product and sent onward as text, so apply the same caution you would to pasting, don't hand over sensitive documents you wouldn't want stored
tools.interview: The friend-version: the core AI model only predicts text, so how can it look at photos, read your PDF, or search the web? Those are extras the product bundles around the engine. Think of the model as an engine and the app as a car built around it, reading files, browsing the internet, doing math, talking out loud, are features the car adds (and a few engines can also see images). When the model needs something beyond text, it calls a tool, a separate program that does the real work and hands the result back as text. So 'can this AI do X?' really means 'does this product give the model a tool for X?', which is exactly why two different AI apps can have very different abilities.

using.mech:
This lesson has no new mechanism, it's the judgment that falls out of all the mechanisms you've already learned, assembled into a five-second habit. Run it before any task. Step one: how capable does the model need to be? You learned models come in sizes, bigger is smarter, slower, pricier; smaller is faster and cheaper. A simple rewrite or brainstorm doesn't need the heavyweight; a subtle analysis might. Right-size it instead of defaulting to the biggest. Many apps add a second dial: a quick mode or a thinking mode that works the problem through before answering. Thinking pays off on hard, multi-step problems and is wasted on a quick rewrite. Step two: roughly how many tokens is this? From the tokens and context lessons you know cost and speed track tokens, and that big pasted inputs and long requested outputs are where the money and the latency live. You don't need exact counts, just the instinct to trim a giant paste and ask for a shorter answer when you can.

Step three: what does being wrong cost me? This is where the limits lesson cashes in. Low-stakes and reversible? Move fast, accept good-enough, skip the heavy verification. High-stakes or hard to undo? Use a stronger model, ground it in real sources, and verify the output yourself, especially specifics and anything recent. And underneath it all sits the one split that prevents most mishaps: trust the model to draft, brainstorm, explain, and rephrase; verify it for facts, numbers, fresh events, and citations. That's the entire course as a reflex. Master it and you're not just using AI, you're ready to start building with it, which is precisely where the Engineering Mastery course begins.
trade: The heavyweight is smarter but slower and pricier; for most everyday tasks a smaller model is the better, cheaper call
Thinking is slower and uses more of your budget or limits; it earns its keep on multi-step problems and adds little to simple asks
Low-stakes work rewards speed and good-enough; high-stakes work demands a stronger model, real sources, and a human check
Lean on it for drafting, brainstorming, and rephrasing; double-check it for facts, numbers, recent claims, and citations
scale: The biggest cost levers for a beginner are model choice, thinking level, and length, picking a smaller model, saving thinking for hard problems, and trimming huge inputs and outputs handles most of your bill
On a monthly app plan, the same levers decide how quickly you hit your usage limits rather than how big your bill is
Surprise costs almost always trace to the same two things from earlier lessons, large pasted documents (input tokens) and long generated answers (output tokens), watch both
You don't need to track tokens precisely; a rough instinct, 'this is a big paste and a long answer, so it'll cost real money', is enough to make good everyday calls
sec: Scale your caution to the stakes, the same tool deserves a relaxed approach for a brainstorm and a careful, verified, human-checked approach for anything medical, legal, financial, or client-facing
Before pasting sensitive data to save effort, ask whether the task actually needs it; treat every input as something the provider could store
When it matters, ground and verify, give the model the real source, ask it to stick to it, and confirm the important claims yourself; that habit prevents the great majority of AI mistakes
using.interview: Here's the whole course in a friend-sized nutshell. Before any task, ask two questions: how capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me? For easy, low-stakes stuff, use a smaller, cheaper, faster model and just go; for hard or high-stakes stuff, use your best model (letting it think first if the problem is genuinely tricky), give it real sources, and check the result yourself. Remember cost tracks tokens, so big pastes and long answers are where the money goes. And keep one simple split in mind, trust it to draft, brainstorm, and rephrase, but verify it on facts, numbers, recent events, and citations. Do that, and you're using AI like a pro, and you're ready to start actually building with it.

whatai.intro: You don't need to code anything in this course, but it helps to see the loop in plain terms. This is the entire idea of how a model writes an answer, written as simple pseudo-code, not a real program. Read it like a recipe.
whatai.code:
text_so_far = your_question

# the model writes the answer one small chunk at a time
repeat:
    next_chunk = model.most_likely_next(text_so_far)   # a fresh guess
    text_so_far = text_so_far + next_chunk             # add it on
    if next_chunk == "[done]":                         # model decides it's finished
        stop

# what you read as a single, fluent answer was actually
# built up guess-by-guess, left to right, just like this.
notes: most_likely_next is the whole model, everything else is just a loop around it. There's no separate step where it checks a fact or searches the web; the next chunk is always just a prediction
The guess depends on text_so_far, the entire conversation up to this point. Change the input even slightly and the predictions change, which is why how you phrase a question matters
The [done] stop is itself a prediction, the model decides an answer is complete the same way it decides any other chunk, so it can stop too early or ramble too long
There's deliberate randomness in the pick, so the same question can produce slightly different answers each run, that's normal, not a malfunction
debug: It stated a 'fact' that turned out to be false
It filled a gap with likely-sounding text (a hallucination) instead of admitting it didn't know
Verify anything that matters against a real source; the smoother the wording, the more carefully you should check
It 'forgot' something I told it earlier
The conversation grew past the model's short-term memory, or it's a brand-new chat
Covered in the context lesson; for now, restate the key detail or start fresh with it included
I asked twice and got two different answers
Built-in randomness, the model makes fresh guesses each time
Expected behavior, not a bug; if you need consistency, ask for it explicitly or pick the better answer yourself

tokens.intro: No coding needed, this is just to make tokenizing concrete. Here, in plain pseudo-code, is the idea of slicing text into tokens and seeing why the count rarely matches the word count. Read it like a recipe, not a program.
tokens.code:
text = "I love tokenization!"

# the model can't read this directly. first it gets chopped:
tokens = tokenize(text)
# -> ["I", " love", " token", "ization", "!"]
#    common word "love" = 1 token
#    rare word "tokenization" = split into " token" + "ization"
#    the space and the "!" are tokens too

print(count(tokens))   # -> 5 tokens, even though it's only 3 words

# cost and length limits are measured in THIS number,
# not in words and not in characters.
notes: tokenize(text) is the hidden first step on every request, you never call it, but it always runs, on your input and on the model's output
Common words map to one token; rare or long words get split, which is why the token count is usually higher than the word count
Spaces and punctuation are tokens too, that's part of why short-looking text can still be a surprising number of tokens
The model predicts the next token, not the next word, so 'how it reads' and 'how it's priced' are the exact same unit
debug: My cost was higher than I expected
A long pasted input or a long answer, both are billed in tokens
Trim the input to what's needed and ask for a shorter answer; check token counts in a tokenizer if it matters
It miscounted the letters in a word
It sees tokens (chunks), not individual characters
Don't trust the model for letter-level tasks; use a tool that actually reads characters
The same text costs more in another language
Many non-English texts split into more tokens for the same meaning
Expected; budget more tokens for those languages, there's no setting to change it

context.intro: No coding needed, this just shows the trick the chat app is doing behind the scenes. In plain pseudo-code, here's how a 'conversation' really works and why things fall out of memory. Read it like a recipe.
context.code:
history = []   # the running conversation

when you send a message:
    history.append(your_message)

    # the app glues the WHOLE history into one block...
    block = join(history)

    # ...but it must fit the context window:
    while count_tokens(block) > WINDOW_SIZE:
        drop_oldest(history)        # earliest messages fall off
        # (some apps squeeze them into a summary instead)
        block = join(history)

    answer = model.respond(block)   # model sees ONLY this block
    history.append(answer)

# the model has no memory of its own — each turn it
# only ever sees the block that still fits the window.
notes: The model is handed the whole history every turn, the feeling of an ongoing chat is the app re-sending everything, not the model remembering
drop_oldest is why early details vanish, once a message falls out of the window, the model literally never receives it again (apps that summarize instead keep the gist but can still lose the details)
Everything shares the same window: history, your message, pasted files, and the answer being written, fill it with one and there's less room for the rest
A bigger WINDOW_SIZE delays the dropping but never removes the limit, and a fuller block is slower and costs more every turn
debug: It forgot something I said much earlier
That message fell out of the context window as the chat grew
Restate the key detail right before you need it, or start a fresh chat with a short summary
It's ignoring most of a long document I pasted
The relevant part is buried, or the document filled the window and crowded things out
Paste only the section that matters and put your question right next to it
A long conversation keeps getting worse
Context drift: early framing dropped off and noise accumulated
Start a new chat, paste a clean summary of what matters, and continue from there

prompting.intro: No coding here, just a way to see what makes a prompt good. Below, in plain pseudo-code, is the difference between a vague prompt and a clear one, and the refine-don't-restart move. Read it like a recipe for briefing an assistant.
prompting.code:
# a vague prompt leaves the answer wide open
ask("write about dogs")
# -> generic, could-be-anything text

# a clear prompt names the task, context, and shape
ask("""
  TASK:    write a welcome blurb
  CONTEXT: for a neighborhood coffee shop's About page,
           aimed at first-time visitors
  FORMAT:  3 sentences, friendly but not cutesy,
           mention we roast our own beans
""")
# -> specific, on-target text

# if it's close but not perfect, refine — don't start over
ask("good — make the first sentence punchier")
notes: The model takes the prompt literally and knows nothing you didn't include, that's why naming the TASK, CONTEXT, and FORMAT works so well
CONTEXT is the part beginners skip most, the audience and goal the model can't possibly guess, adding it is usually the biggest single upgrade
FORMAT (length, tone, structure) turns 'a fine answer' into 'the answer I wanted', if you don't say it, the model just guesses
The final line is the key habit: refine in small steps instead of rewriting from scratch, your feedback becomes part of the prompt and steers the next try
debug: The answer is generic and bland
The prompt was too vague, the model filled the gaps with safe, average text
Add the task, the context (audience/goal), and the format you want, then send again
It answered a slightly different question than I meant
It took your wording literally
Restate the ask more precisely; spell out exactly what you want done
It's the right idea but the wrong shape or length
You didn't specify format
Just ask: 'in three bullets', 'one short paragraph', 'more formal tone', it'll happily reshape it
It keeps dropping one of my requirements
Too much packed into one prompt and one got lost
Pull that requirement out and handle it as a separate follow-up step

chat.intro: No coding needed, this just exposes the trick the chat app plays to fake memory. In plain pseudo-code, here's what really happens every time you send a message. Read it like a recipe, not a program.
chat.code:
transcript = [system_message]   # hidden 'be a helpful assistant' line
# (+ your custom instructions and any memory notes, if those are on)

when you send a message:
    transcript.append(your_message)

    # glue the WHOLE transcript into one block, every turn
    block = join(transcript)

    # the model has NO memory — it only sees this block
    reply = model.respond(block)

    transcript.append(reply)

# a NEW chat just means: transcript = [system_message]
# (empty of history) — which is why it knows nothing
# about your other conversations, apart from any notes
# a memory feature slips back in.
notes: The model is stateless, every turn it gets the whole transcript fresh and forgets right after, the 'memory' is the app re-sending everything
The hidden system_message sits at the top of every block, it's why an assistant has a consistent personality and rules you never typed
A new chat is literally a transcript reset to just the system message, that's the whole reason it can't see your earlier conversations
A memory feature (like custom instructions or a project brief) is just an extra line that inserts saved notes into the transcript before sending, the model still didn't learn anything
debug: A new chat doesn't know about my last one
Each chat is a separate transcript that starts empty
Expected; paste in or restate anything you need carried over, or turn on a memory feature if the product has one
It forgot what we agreed earlier in a long chat
That part dropped out of the context window, so it's no longer in the transcript
Restate the key point, or start fresh with a short summary at the top
It has a personality or rules I didn't ask for
A hidden system message is shaping every reply
That's the product's built-in brief; a different tool has a different one, you can't usually see it
The memory feature stored something odd about me
It saved a note from an earlier chat and keeps inserting it
Check the product's memory settings, you can usually view, edit, or delete what it saved

limits.intro: No coding needed, this shows in plain terms why a model invents answers and why it's stuck in the past. Read the pseudo-code like a recipe for what the engine does when it hits a gap.
limits.code:
# the model's only move: produce the most likely next text
answer = most_likely_text(prompt)

# there's NO separate fact-check step like this:
#   if i_dont_actually_know(prompt):
#       say("I don't know")        # <- this doesn't exist
#
# "I'm not sure" only comes out when it happens to be the
# most likely text. so when it lacks the real answer, it
# often outputs the most plausible-SOUNDING text instead
#   -> a HALLUCINATION.

# and its knowledge is frozen at training time:
if question_is_after(KNOWLEDGE_CUTOFF):
    # it has no data for this... but answers anyway,
    # from an out-of-date world, just as confidently.
    pass
notes: There's no separate fact-check step, the model emits the most likely text, so unless 'I'm not sure' happens to be the likeliest reply, a gap tends to become a confident fabrication, not a blank
Hallucination is worst on specifics (quotes, numbers, citations, links) about niche topics, that's where 'sounds right' and 'is right' drift furthest apart
KNOWLEDGE_CUTOFF is a hard wall: anything after it simply wasn't in training, and the model usually can't tell that your question crosses it
Grounding fixes a lot, give it the real source ('answer only from this text') and the likely-next-text is anchored to facts instead of thin air
debug: It gave me a quote/statistic/citation
It may have fabricated a realistic-looking detail to fill a gap
Verify it actually exists before using it; the more specific and authoritative it looks, the more carefully check
It answered confidently about a recent event
The event may be after its knowledge cutoff, so it's guessing from old data
Check the date; for anything recent, use a search tool or a real source, not the model's memory
It contradicted itself between two answers
It was generating plausible text, not drawing on one stable fact
Treat both as unverified; go check an authoritative source
It doubled down when I pushed back
Confidence isn't evidence, even under pressure
Don't be persuaded by insistence; verify independently
It cited a source, but the source doesn't say that
The model attached a real link to a claim it got wrong or stretched
Open the source and find the exact passage; if it isn't there, treat the claim as unverified

tools.intro: No coding needed, this shows the simple pattern behind 'AI that can do anything'. In plain pseudo-code, here's how a model uses a tool when a task is beyond plain text. Read it like a recipe.
tools.code:
# the bare model only predicts text. for real-world
# tasks, the product gives it TOOLS it can call.

when the model hits something it can't do alone:
    if needs_current_info:
        result = web_search(query)      # a tool fetches fresh text
    if needs_exact_math:
        result = calculator(numbers)    # a tool does the real math
    if you_attached_a_file:
        result = read_file(file)        # converts it: text, maybe page images

    # the tool's result is pasted back into the prompt
    # as TEXT, and the model continues from there.
    answer = model.respond(prompt + result)

# 'can this AI do X?'  ==  'does this product
# give the model a TOOL for X?'
notes: The engine never changes, it's always the same text predictor; tools are separate helpers the product wires up around it
A tool's result comes back as text in the prompt, that's how the model 'uses' a calculator or a search without doing the work itself
This is why capabilities vary by product: image input, web search, and file reading are features that may or may not be bundled in
Reading a file means the app converted it first (the text, and in some apps page images), so a messy scan or photo can come through garbled or not at all
debug: It couldn't read my PDF
It may be a scan or photo this app can't read cleanly, or too long for the window
Try a text-based file, paste the relevant text directly, use clearer scans, or trim it to the part that matters
It gave outdated info even though it can browse
Search may not have actually run that turn
Ask it explicitly to search, and look for a source link confirming it pulled fresh information
It got the math wrong
The plain text model was guessing the number
Use a calculator/tool feature, or have it show the steps so you can verify, don't trust raw mental math
A feature works in one AI app but not another
Different products bundle different tools
The capability isn't part of every model; pick a product whose features fit your task

using.intro: No coding needed, this is the whole course distilled into a checklist you run before a task. In plain pseudo-code, here's the habit for choosing a model and deciding how much to trust the answer. Read it like a recipe.
using.code:
before each task:

    # 1. how capable does the model need to be?
    if task_is_simple:
        model = small_fast_cheap        # don't overpay
    else:
        model = bigger_more_capable
    if task_is_hard_and_multi_step:
        thinking = on                   # slower, but works it through

    # 2. roughly how many tokens? (cost & speed)
    trim(huge_pasted_inputs)
    ask_for(shorter_answer_when_possible)

    # 3. what does being wrong cost me?
    if low_stakes:
        go_fast()                       # good-enough is fine
    else:
        give_real_sources()             # ground it
        verify_output_yourself()        # esp. facts & recent

# verify it on: facts, numbers, recent events, citations
notes: Right-size the model, the biggest one is slower and pricier and overkill for most tasks; reach for it only when the work is genuinely hard, and turn thinking on only for hard, multi-step problems
Cost tracks tokens, big pasted inputs and long answers are where the money goes, so trimming both is your main everyday lever
Scale caution to stakes, fast and good-enough for low-stakes, but ground-and-verify for anything high-stakes or hard to undo
The bottom two lines are the single most useful split in the whole course: trust it to generate, verify it on facts

You may be on the heavyweight model for a simple task, or sending huge inputs
Drop to a smaller model and trim big pastes and long outputs; right-size both
I'm unsure whether to trust an answer

My tool can't do something I need
It may lack that feature (search, files, images)
Pick a product whose bundled capabilities match the task
It answered fast, but the reasoning falls apart
A hard multi-step problem got a quick-mode answer
Switch on thinking or a higher effort setting, ask again, and check the steps
I want to build with this, not just chat
Foundations is about using models; building is the next step
