whatai.q: Your friend says, "The AI is basically a smart search engine, it looks up the answer and shows it to you." What's the most accurate correction?
o: It's really just search with a chat box on top, looking up the matching page
On its own it doesn't look anything up, it generates new text by predicting what comes next
It quietly searches a private company database that's hidden from the public web
It memorized every webpage word-for-word and reads back the one that matches you
whatai.exp: A search engine finds existing pages; a language model generates fresh text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next chunk. That's why it can write something brand new, and also why it can make things up. Many apps now add a search step on top, but that's an added feature, not what the model does on its own.

whatai.q: A model gives you a beautifully written, confident answer about a niche topic. What does that confidence tell you about whether it's correct?
o: Confident, fluent wording is a strong signal that the answer is very likely correct
Confidence means it pulled the answer from a reliable, checked-over source somewhere
Almost nothing, fluency is the model's goal and is unrelated to accuracy
It means the fact was in its training data, so the answer is already verified for you
whatai.exp: The model is built to produce text that reads well, so it phrases a wrong answer just as smoothly as a right one. Confidence in the wording is not evidence. For anything that matters, you verify it independently.

whatai.q: Why might a model confidently invent a fact, like a fake statistic or a quote that was never said?
o: Something glitched inside the model, and a quick restart on your end would clear the made-up fact right up
A person deliberately loaded that exact false information into the model to trip you and other users up
Its job is to produce likely-sounding text, so when it lacks the real answer it fills the gap with a plausible guess
It actually knows the real truth but is bending it on purpose to come across as more helpful to you here
whatai.exp: This is called a hallucination. Because the model always tries to produce the most likely next text, a gap in what it learned gets filled with something that sounds right rather than something that is right. It's a side effect of how the engine works, not a fixable glitch.

whatai.q: You ask a model the same question twice and get two slightly different answers. What's going on?
o: One of the two answers is simply a malfunction that you happened to catch this time
The model is quietly rewriting and updating itself in real time as the two of you chat
Normal behavior, it makes fresh guesses each time, so wording can vary
It recalled that you weren't happy with the first reply and reworded it to please you
whatai.exp: The model assembles each answer on the spot, guess by guess, and there's deliberate variation built in. Getting two different-but-reasonable answers is expected, not a sign anything is wrong.

whatai.q: Which of these tasks plays directly to what a language model is genuinely good at?
o: Telling you today's local weather on its own, with no tools
Rephrasing a rough email into a clear, polite version
Recalling word-for-word what you said last week, memory off
Multiplying two huge numbers with a guaranteed-exact result
whatai.exp: Rewriting and rephrasing is pure text generation, the model's home turf. The other three depend on things it can't do alone: live data, persistent memory, or exact arithmetic. Knowing the difference is the practical payoff of this whole lesson.

tokens.q: What is a token, in the way an AI model uses the word?
o: Always exactly one whole English word, no more and no less, every single time
A small chunk of text, often a word-piece, that the model reads and writes
A single letter of the alphabet that the model lines up one after another
A secret password you have to enter before the model will unlock and respond
tokens.exp: A token is a small chunk of text, often a common word, a word-piece, a space, or a punctuation mark. As a rough rule it's about three-quarters of a word. The model reads and writes in these chunks rather than in whole words or individual letters.

tokens.q: Why does the word count of your message rarely match its token count?
o: They line up perfectly because one token is always exactly one word, so the two counts will match every single time
The model quietly slips in extra invisible tokens on purpose just to inflate the amount you end up billed
Common words are one token, but longer or rarer words split into several, and spaces and punctuation count too
Token counting is buggy and unreliable on its own, so the numbers you actually see are basically meaningless
tokens.exp: Short common words map to a single token, but longer or unusual words get broken into pieces, and spaces and punctuation are their own tokens. So the token count is usually a bit higher than the word count, and the two rarely line up exactly.

tokens.q: A model struggles to tell you how many times the letter 's' appears in 'Mississippi.' What's the best explanation?
o: Something is broken inside the model, and a fresh software update would fix the miscounting
It reads text as tokens (chunks), not as individual letters, so letter-level tasks are genuinely hard for it
The word is simply too short for the model to take in and process properly the way it needs to
It actually can do this just fine but is choosing to refuse the small task only to be difficult
tokens.exp: The model sees chunks like 'Miss' and 'issippi', not the separate letters. Counting specific characters means reasoning about something it can't directly see, so it's a real weak spot. For letter-perfect tasks, use a tool that actually reads characters.

tokens.q: You have a short question but you paste a 20-page document along with it. What happens to the token count?
o: Only the words in your question count, and anything extra you paste in just rides along for free with it
The pasted document is input tokens too, so the total is large even though your question is short
Pasting a big block of text actually shrinks the count by giving the model a head start
Tokens only ever apply to the model's written answer, never to anything you send it
tokens.exp: Everything you send in is input tokens, including pasted documents. A short question with a big paste can use a lot of tokens, which means more cost and a slower response. Trimming to the part that matters is the fix.

tokens.q: When you pay per use (the way builders and many work tools are billed), which statement about cost is accurate?
o: Only the text you type is counted, and the model's whole reply comes back to you for free
Only the model's reply gets counted, and everything you send into it costs you nothing
Both your input and the model's reply count as tokens, and the reply is often the bigger half
Every message costs the same flat amount, however long the question or the answer runs
tokens.exp: Both input tokens (what you send) and output tokens (what the model writes back) are counted, and the answer is frequently the larger and more expensive half. That's why asking for a shorter answer can meaningfully cut cost and time. On a flat monthly app plan you won't see this as a bill, but heavy token use tends to show up as hitting your usage limits sooner.

o: A little pop-up box in the chat app where extra options and settings appear
The maximum amount of text, in tokens, a model can look at in one go
The model's permanent long-term memory holding everything you've ever told it
A setting you flip on to make the model slow down, think harder, and try more
context.exp: The context window is the cap on how much text the model can take in at once, measured in tokens. It has to hold the conversation so far, your current message, any pasted files, and the answer being written, all at the same time.

context.q: In a long conversation, the model 'forgets' something you said near the start. What most likely happened?
o: The model gradually lost interest in the chat partway through and just quietly stopped paying any real attention to you
The conversation grew past the context window, so the earliest messages were dropped and the model no longer receives them
The model is deliberately punishing you for sending it far too many long-winded messages in a row
A hiccup somewhere in your internet connection quietly wiped that earlier message before it ever arrived
context.exp: As a chat grows beyond the window, the oldest messages stop being included in what the model is sent. From its point of view this turn, those messages were never there, so it can't refer to them. Restating the detail brings it back.

context.q: Does the model remember your conversation on its own between turns?
o: Yes, it quietly keeps a private long-term memory of every single message you've ever exchanged with it
No, the app re-sends the whole conversation each turn, and the model only sees what fits in the window
Yes, but that saved memory only switches on for you once you upgrade to one of the paid plans
No, it forgets each message the very instant you hit send and then answers you completely blindly
context.exp: The model has no memory of its own between turns. The feeling of an ongoing chat comes from the app gluing the whole history together and re-sending it every time. The model only ever works with the block of text it's handed, as long as it fits the window.

context.q: You paste an entire long report and ask a precise question about one line buried in it. Why might the answer disappoint you?
o: Pasting any document in always overloads the model and breaks its ability to answer
The key detail can get buried in a crowded window, so the model may latch onto the wrong thing
The model flatly refuses to read documents and only handles short typed questions
Longer documents actually make the model both faster and more accurate every time
context.exp: More text isn't automatically better. When the window is packed with mostly-irrelevant material, the one line that matters is easy to miss. Giving the model just the relevant section, with your question right beside it, usually works far better.

context.q: A conversation has gotten very long and the model's answers are drifting. What's a reliable fix?
o: Just keep the same chat going and trust that it will quietly steer itself back on track
Type your next message in all capital letters so the model finally pays proper attention
Start a fresh chat and paste in a short summary of what actually matters
Ask the very same question over and over in a row until one of the tries comes out right
context.exp: Drift happens as early context drops off and noise piles up in the window. Starting a clean chat with a concise summary puts just the relevant information back in front of the model, which usually restores accuracy. You control what's in the window.

o: A secret password phrase that quietly unlocks the model's better, hidden answers it keeps in reserve
The text you give the model to work with, your instruction plus any context you include
A hidden setting you switch on that makes the model itself smarter and more capable
The model's finished reply, the answer it hands back after reading your question
prompting.exp: A prompt is simply the input you send the model: your question or instruction, plus any context or examples. It's everything the model has to work from, so whatever you leave out, it doesn't know. Writing clear prompts is the highest-leverage skill in the course.

prompting.q: Your prompt is just "write something about our app." Why is the result likely to be generic?
o: The model is just feeling lazy this time and isn't really putting in its full effort for you here
The prompt is too vague, with no task, audience, or format, so the model fills the gaps with safe, average text
You forgot to include the special command words the model needs before it will actually begin writing
The model simply doesn't know nearly enough about apps to write anything genuinely useful about one
prompting.exp: A vague prompt leaves the most-likely continuation wide open, so the model drifts toward bland, could-be-anything text. Adding the specific task, the audience and goal, and the format you want narrows it down and gets you a far more useful answer.

prompting.q: The first answer is close to what you wanted but a bit too long and too formal. What's the best next move?
o: Throw the reply out and start fresh with a brand-new, much fuller prompt
Just give up on it, since this proves the model can't handle the task
Reply with a small refinement, like 'shorter and a bit more casual'
Send the very same prompt again and simply hope for better luck this time
prompting.exp: Prompting is a back-and-forth. When an answer is close, refining with a small instruction is faster and more reliable than rewriting from scratch. Your feedback becomes part of the prompt and steers the next attempt toward what you actually want.

prompting.q: Why does pasting in one good example of the format you want often work so well?
o: It quietly tricks the model into deciding to try a good deal harder than it normally bothers to
Continuing a concrete pattern is exactly what the model is best at, so an example teaches it the shape fast
Examples are flat-out required every time, and without one the model simply won't send you any reply
It makes no real difference to the result at all, since only your written instructions actually matter
prompting.exp: The model predicts text by continuing patterns, so a concrete example dropped into the prompt is a pattern it can follow directly. One good 'like this' sample often communicates format and tone more precisely than a paragraph of description.

prompting.q: Which mindset best describes good prompting?
o: Collecting magic phrases that you recite to force the model into giving you its good answers
Arguing and pushing back at the model over and over until it finally gives in to you
Briefing a capable new assistant: say the task, give the context, describe a good result
Keeping every prompt as short as you possibly can, no matter what you're asking for
prompting.exp: The model takes your words literally and can't read your mind, so the winning mindset is briefing a sharp assistant on day one: state the task, supply the context they'd need, and describe what a good answer looks like. It's clear instructions, not secret tricks.

chat.q: What does it mean that a language model is 'stateless'?
o: It keeps a permanent file of every chat you've had, ready to recall on its own
It keeps no memory between turns, each message is handled on its own
It can follow only one topic at a time, forgetting the moment you switch
It runs on a special computer that quietly saves your history for later
chat.exp: Stateless means the model remembers nothing between turns, each request is handled as if it were the first thing you'd ever said. Any sense of an ongoing conversation comes from outside the model, not from the model itself.

chat.q: If the model has no memory, how does a chat seem to 'remember' what you said earlier?
o: The model quietly tucks each of your earlier messages away inside its own private memory
The chat app re-sends the entire conversation so far, as one block, every turn
It makes an educated guess about what you most likely said earlier
It doesn't really remember, each reply is just picked at random
chat.exp: The chat app keeps a transcript and re-sends the whole thing, your messages and the model's replies, each turn, with your new message added. The model re-reads that transcript every time. The continuity is in the re-sent text, not in the model recalling anything.

chat.q: You start a brand-new chat and it knows nothing about your previous conversation. Why?
o: Something is broken and the app failed to load your earlier history
A new chat starts a fresh transcript, and with no memory notes added, nothing from earlier is in it
The model has quietly decided to ignore the things you told it in your earlier conversations
You forgot to log in, so the app hasn't linked any of your past conversations to this one yet
chat.exp: Each chat is its own separate transcript. A new one starts empty apart from the hidden system message (plus any notes a memory feature or your custom instructions add), so the model has nothing else about your other conversations. That's expected, not a bug.

chat.q: A product's 'memory' feature remembers your name and preferences across chats. What's actually happening?
o: The model permanently learned those new facts and rewrote part of itself to keep them around
An extra feature saves notes about you and slips them into the transcript, the model itself didn't change
The model is quietly reading your mind each time to recall your name and your saved details
Nothing real is happening at all, these memory features only pretend to remember you across chats
chat.exp: A memory feature is a layer built on top of the model: it stores notes about you and quietly inserts them into the conversation. The model didn't learn anything, the app just put the note in front of it. You can usually view and edit what it saved.

chat.q: Many chat tools add a hidden instruction at the very top of the transcript. What is it for?
o: To slow the model down on purpose so that its answers arrive a little more slowly and carefully
To tell the model how to behave (its role, tone, and rules), shaping every answer in the chat
To store your account password safely, pinned right at the very top of the chat
It's just leftover text from setup that has no real effect on the answers you get
chat.exp: That's the system message: a behind-the-scenes instruction pinned to the top of every turn, telling the model how to act ('you are a helpful assistant'). You don't see it, but it's part of the transcript each turn and shapes the tone and rules of the whole conversation.

limits.q: An app searched the web and gave you an answer with three source links. For something that matters, what's the smartest next step?
o: Trust it fully, since an answer that comes with links can't contain made-up facts
Open the sources and check that they really say what the answer claims
Ignore the links, since search results are always less reliable than memory
Ask the same question again and keep whichever answer sounds most confident
limits.exp: Search cuts down on made-up facts, but it doesn't make an answer bulletproof: the model can misread a page, lean on a weak source, or attach a real link to a claim the page doesn't actually make. A quick click-through on the sources that matter is how you catch it.

limits.q: Why can't hallucination simply be switched off completely?
o: The companies behind these models simply don't care quite enough to bother actually fixing the problem
It comes from the same machinery that makes the model useful, always producing likely-sounding text
It only ever shows up on the cheap free models, never on the expensive flagship ones
It already can be, there's a single setting that guarantees the model never makes a mistake
limits.exp: Hallucination is a side effect of the core behavior: always generating the most plausible next text. You can reduce it with better prompts, real sources, and asking for citations, but there's no setting that guarantees the model never makes anything up.

o: A daily limit on how many questions you're allowed to ask the model before the count finally resets again
The date a model's training data stops, after which it knows nothing unless a tool feeds it fresh info
The point in a long chat where the model gets tired and its answers start slipping in quality
A premium upgrade you pay extra each month to unlock sharper, fuller, more detailed answers
limits.exp: The knowledge cutoff is the date the model's training data ends. It knows nothing about events, prices, or releases after that point, and often can't tell exactly when its own cutoff is, so it may answer recent questions confidently from an outdated world.

limits.q: A model gives you a confident answer about something that happened last week. What's the safest assumption?
o: If it sounds this confident and specific, the answer is almost certainly current and correct
It may be past the model's knowledge cutoff, so it could be guessing from old data unless a search tool ran
Models stay automatically up to date behind the scenes, so any recent answer is always safe to trust
It quietly refreshed its own training overnight, so it now knows everything that happened last week
limits.exp: Recent events may fall after the model's cutoff, where it has no real data, yet it still answers confidently. Unless you can confirm a search tool fetched fresh information, treat anything recent as possibly out of date and verify it against a current source.

limits.q: Which type of answer most deserves a careful double-check?
o: A loose brainstorm of creative ideas where being a little off the mark costs you nothing
A simple request to reword, shorten, or tidy up a paragraph you have already written yourself by hand
Specific, copyable details, exact statistics, named quotes, citations, links, on a niche or recent topic
A plain-language explanation of a common, well-known concept most people already understand
limits.exp: Hallucination is most likely and most dangerous on precise, verifiable details about obscure or recent topics, exactly the things that look authoritative and are tempting to copy. Those are the answers to verify first. Drafting and rephrasing carry far less risk.

tools.q: The core language model only predicts text. So how can an AI app look at a photo or search the web?
o: The model secretly has every one of those abilities already built inside it
Modern products bundle extra abilities (tools) around the text engine
It can't really, those photo and web features are just clever fakes
It quietly downloads a fresh, more capable brain for each new task
tools.exp: Think of the model as an engine and the product as a car built around it. Seeing images, reading files, browsing the web, and doing math are features the product adds. When the model needs one, it calls a tool that does the real work and returns the result as text.

tools.q: You attach a PDF and the AI summarizes it. What actually happened?
o: The model reached into your device on its own and opened the original file in a reader app
The app converted the file into text (and in some apps page images) and put it in the prompt
The model memorized the whole PDF permanently so it can answer questions about it later
The PDF was quietly emailed off to a human assistant who wrote the summary for you
tools.exp: Reading a file means the app pulled the content out, the text and, in some apps, pictures of each page, and added it to the prompt. The model is reading that converted version, not 'opening' the document, which is why a scan or a photo of a page can work in one app and stump another.

tools.q: What is a 'tool,' in the sense used in this lesson?
o: A button tucked away somewhere deep inside the app's own settings menu that you flip on to turn its features on
An outside helper the model can call, like a calculator, web search, or file reader, that returns text
Just another name people use when they mean the underlying language model itself
A physical device you plug into your computer to give the AI more raw power
tools.exp: A tool is any external helper the model can call when a task is beyond plain text prediction: a calculator, a search engine, a code runner, a database. The model requests it, the tool does the exact work, and the result comes back as text the model uses.

tools.q: Why does giving the model a calculator tool make it more reliable at math?
o: It nudges the model to slow right down and think much harder about each of the numbers it sees
The calculator does the exact arithmetic, replacing the model's shaky guess with a real answer
It doesn't actually help at all, and adding tools like this tends to make the math worse
It teaches the model the arithmetic for good, so it gets the math right on its own next time
tools.exp: On its own, the text engine only guesses a plausible-looking number. A calculator tool actually computes the exact result and hands it back. Tools are how products patch over the model's weak spots, math, fresh info, exact lookups, without changing the engine itself.

tools.q: A feature you love in one AI app isn't available in another. What's the most likely reason?
o: The second app simply runs on a fundamentally different and clearly much worse underlying engine
Different products bundle different tools, the capability isn't part of every model
You're simply using the second app the wrong way and missing it
That feature was taken down from the internet and no longer exists
tools.exp: The underlying text engine is similar across products; what differs is which tools and capabilities each one wires up (search, image input, file reading). So 'can this AI do X?' really means 'does this product give the model a tool for X?'

using.q: For a quick, low-stakes task like brainstorming names, which model is usually the smart choice?
o: Always reach for the biggest, most powerful model you can possibly get
A smaller, faster, cheaper model, it's plenty for simple work
It honestly doesn't matter, every model costs about the same to run
Pick whichever one is most expensive, just to be on the safe side
using.exp: Bigger models are smarter but slower and pricier, and they're overkill for simple tasks. Right-sizing, using a small, fast, cheap model for easy work and saving the heavyweight (and deep thinking) for genuinely hard problems, is the core habit of using AI well.

using.q: You need help with a genuinely hard, multi-step problem, like planning a budget around several competing constraints. Which setup is most likely to help?
o: A thinking or higher-effort mode that works the problem through before answering
The quickest mode available, since a faster answer is always the more accurate one
Any mode at all, since every setting runs exactly the same reasoning behind the scenes
Splitting it into many tiny chats so the model never sees all the constraints together
using.exp: Thinking modes have the model work through the problem (breaking it down, trying an approach, checking it) before answering. That's slower and uses more of your budget or limits, but it pays off on multi-step problems like math, planning, and tricky analysis. For a quick rewrite or a simple question, the fast mode is the better call.

using.q: What two questions best decide how much care a task needs?
o: How fast can I type this out, and roughly how long will the model's answer run on for?
How capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me?
Which model is the newest release, and which one is the cheapest?
Is the AI service online right now, and is my internet fast enough?
using.exp: These two questions, capability needed and cost of being wrong, right-size both your model choice and your caution. Cheap-and-fast for low stakes; stronger model, real sources, and verification for high stakes. That's the whole course as a five-second habit.

using.q: Which split best captures when to trust the model versus when to verify it?
o: Trust it completely for any math you give it; double-check only its spelling and grammar
Trust it to draft, brainstorm, explain, and rephrase; verify it on facts, numbers, and citations
Trust every single word it tells you as true, and never waste your time verifying anything
Verify every answer equally and just as carefully, no matter how trivial or low-stakes the task
using.exp: The model shines at generation, drafting, brainstorming, explaining, rephrasing, so you can lean on it there. It's least reliable on facts, numbers, recent events, and citations, so verify those. This single split prevents the great majority of AI mishaps.

using.q: You've finished this course and want to go from using these models to building real things with them. What's the next step?
o: Nothing more, you've already learned everything that these models could ever possibly offer you
The Engineering Mastery course, which picks up exactly where Foundations ends
Just keep chatting away until you eventually figure the rest out
Start this same Foundations course over again from the beginning
using.exp: Foundations gave you the mental models for using AI; building with it, designing prompts at scale, wiring up tools, controlling cost in real systems, is the Engineering Mastery course, which assumes everything you learned here. It's the natural next step.

CARDS.f: In one sentence, what is a large language model?
CARDS.b: A text-prediction machine: you give it text, and it repeatedly guesses the most likely next chunk until it has written a full answer. Think of it as a very well-read autocomplete.

CARDS.f: Does a language model look up facts in a database?
CARDS.b: No. On its own it generates new text by predicting what comes next, it isn't retrieving stored facts or searching the web (some apps add a search step on top). That's why it can be creative and also why it can make things up.

CARDS.f: Why does a confident-sounding answer not mean a correct answer?
CARDS.b: The model's goal is fluent-sounding text, so it phrases wrong answers just as smoothly as right ones. Confidence is unrelated to accuracy, verify anything that matters.

CARDS.f: What is a hallucination?
CARDS.b: When the model fills a gap in what it learned with plausible-sounding but false text, like a fake quote or invented statistic. It's a side effect of always predicting likely text, not a bug you can fully switch off.

CARDS.f: Is the model learning from your conversation as you chat?
CARDS.b: No. Its training finished before you ever used it, so chatting doesn't change the model you're talking to, and on its own it doesn't remember you between conversations. (Companies may use chats to train future versions if your settings allow it.)

CARDS.f: What is a "thinking" mode actually doing?
CARDS.b: The same text predictor, writing out working notes (breaking the problem down, trying an approach, checking it) before it writes the answer. Slower and uses more tokens, but better on hard, multi-step problems. The notes are still predicted text, not a mind at work.

CARDS.f: What is a token?
CARDS.b: The small chunk of text a model actually reads and writes, often a word, a word-piece, or punctuation. Rough rule: about four characters, or three-quarters of a word. Models read in tokens, not letters or whole words.

CARDS.f: Why does the model struggle to count the letters in a word?
CARDS.b: Because it reads tokens (chunks like ' token' + 'ization'), not individual letters. Letter-level tasks (counting characters, exact spelling, reversing words) are a genuine weak spot, use a real tool instead.

CARDS.f: What gets counted toward cost: your input, the model's output, or both?
CARDS.b: Both. Input tokens are everything you send (including pasted text); output tokens are everything the model writes back. The answer is often the bigger, pricier half, so asking for shorter answers saves money and time.

CARDS.f: Do images, files, and "thinking" use tokens?
CARDS.b: Yes. Pictures, audio, and attachments are converted into tokens too, and a thinking mode's working notes count as output tokens even when you never see them. All of it takes up room and adds cost or usage.

CARDS.f: Why do common words cost fewer tokens than rare ones?
CARDS.b: Common words usually map to a single token; longer or unusual words get split into several pieces. That's also why token counts run a bit higher than word counts, spaces and punctuation count too.

CARDS.f: What is the context window?
CARDS.b: The maximum amount of text (in tokens) a model can look at in one go. It must hold the whole conversation, your message, any pasted files, and the answer, all at once. Think of it as the model's desk, with an edge.

CARDS.f: Why does a model 'forget' something from early in a long chat?
CARDS.b: The conversation grew past the context window, so the earliest messages were dropped from what the model is sent. It's not choosing to forget, it simply never receives those messages this turn. Restate the detail to bring it back.

CARDS.f: Does the model remember the conversation on its own between turns?
CARDS.b: No. It has no memory of its own. The app re-sends the whole history every turn, and the model only sees what fits in the window. The 'ongoing chat' feeling is the app, not the model remembering.

CARDS.f: What happens when a chat outgrows the context window?
CARDS.b: Something has to give. Depending on the app, the oldest messages are dropped, condensed into a summary, or you're asked to start a new chat. Either way, early details can be lost, so restate anything that matters.

CARDS.f: What is retrieval?
CARDS.b: When you give an app more material than fits in the window, it searches that material and puts only the most relevant pieces in front of the model for each question. Handy for big projects, but the model can miss what it never pulled in.

CARDS.f: Is a bigger context window always better?
CARDS.b: No. More room lets you include more, but a fuller window is slower, costs more, and can bury the important detail in noise. A focused, relevant context usually beats a giant one.

CARDS.f: What is a prompt?
CARDS.b: The text you give the model to work with: your instruction or question plus any context or examples. It's everything the model has, and it takes it literally, so whatever you leave out, it doesn't know.

CARDS.f: What three things turn a vague prompt into a good one?
CARDS.b: The task (what you want done), the context (audience, goal, background the model can't guess), and the format (length, tone, structure of a good answer). Add an example when you have one.

CARDS.f: The first answer is close but not right. What's the move?
CARDS.b: Refine, don't restart. Reply with one small instruction ('shorter', 'warmer', 'focus on point two'). Prompting is a back-and-forth, and your feedback steers the next try. Refining is usually faster than rewriting.

CARDS.f: What's the right mindset for prompting?
CARDS.b: Briefing a capable new assistant on day one: say the task, give the context they'd need, and describe a good result. It's clear instructions, not secret magic phrases. The model can't read your mind.

CARDS.f: What does 'stateless' mean for a model?
CARDS.b: It keeps no memory between turns, each message is handled on its own, as if it were the first. Any sense of an ongoing conversation comes from outside the model, not the model itself.

CARDS.f: If the model has no memory, how does chat seem to remember?
CARDS.b: The chat app re-sends the entire conversation so far, your messages and its replies, as one block every turn, with your new message added. The model re-reads that transcript each time. The memory is in the re-sent text, not the model.

CARDS.f: Why does a brand-new chat know nothing about your last one?
CARDS.b: Each chat is its own transcript, and a new one starts empty (apart from a hidden system message). There's nothing from earlier chats for the model to see unless a memory feature, often on by default now, slips notes in.

CARDS.f: What is a system message?
CARDS.b: A hidden instruction most chat tools pin to the very top of the transcript, telling the model how to behave ('you are a helpful assistant') and often giving it today's date. You don't see it, but it shapes the tone and rules of every answer.

CARDS.f: How do custom instructions and projects work?
CARDS.b: You write a standing brief once (about you, your preferences, or a project, maybe with files), and the app re-inserts it into every chat in that space, like your own system message. The model isn't remembering; the app is re-sending your notes.

CARDS.f: What does a temporary (incognito) chat do?
CARDS.b: It isn't saved to your history, doesn't feed the memory feature, and isn't used to train future models. The company may still keep it briefly for safety checks, so it's more private, not invisible.

CARDS.f: What is a hallucination?
CARDS.b: When the model states something false as if it were true, a fake quote, an invented statistic, a citation to a paper that doesn't exist. It fills gaps with plausible text instead of admitting it doesn't know, and no setting fully turns it off.

CARDS.f: What is the knowledge cutoff?
CARDS.b: The date a model's training data stops. It knows nothing about events, prices, or releases after that point, and often can't tell where its own cutoff is, so it may answer recent questions confidently from an outdated world.

CARDS.f: Which answers most deserve a double-check?
CARDS.b: Specific, copyable details, exact statistics, named quotes, citations, links, on niche or recent topics. That's where hallucination is most likely and most tempting to copy. Confidence is never a safety check.

CARDS.f: An answer came with source links. Is it safe now?
CARDS.b: Safer, not safe. Search cuts down on made-up facts, but the model can misread a page or attach a real link to a claim the page doesn't make. For anything that matters, open the source and find the claim yourself.

CARDS.f: What is grounding, and why does it help?
CARDS.b: Giving the model the real source to answer from (paste the document, or use a search tool) instead of asking from memory. The answer is then anchored to actual material, so it's far less likely to be made up.

CARDS.f: The core model only predicts text, so how can it see images or search the web?
CARDS.b: Products bundle extra abilities (tools) around the engine. Think of the model as an engine and the app as a car built around it, vision, search, file reading, and math are features the car adds and calls when needed.

CARDS.f: What is a 'tool' in AI?
CARDS.b: An outside helper the model can call when a task is beyond text prediction, a calculator, web search, file reader, code runner. The tool does the real work and hands the result back as text the model uses.

CARDS.f: Is voice mode a different, smarter AI?
CARDS.b: No. Some voice modes turn your speech into text and read the answer aloud; others hear audio directly and reply faster. Either way it's the same kind of assistant underneath, so it can be just as confidently wrong, only out loud.

CARDS.f: Should you trust the AI summary at the top of search results?
CARDS.b: Give it the same quick check as any AI answer. It's the same kind of engine with the same limits, so click through to the sources for anything that matters.

CARDS.f: Why does 'can this AI do X?' depend on the product, not just the model?
CARDS.b: The engine is similar everywhere; what differs is which tools each product wires up (search, images, files). So the real question is 'does this product give the model a tool for X?', which is why two AI apps can have very different abilities.

CARDS.f: What two questions decide how much care a task needs?
CARDS.b: How capable does the model need to be, and how much does being wrong cost me? Cheap-and-fast for low stakes; stronger model, real sources, and verification for high stakes. That's the whole course as a quick habit.

CARDS.f: When should you trust the model versus verify it?
CARDS.b: Trust it to draft, brainstorm, explain, and rephrase. Verify it on facts, numbers, recent events, and citations. This single split prevents most AI mishaps.

CARDS.f: When is a thinking mode worth it?
CARDS.b: For genuinely hard, multi-step problems: math, planning, tricky analysis, code. It's slower and uses more of your budget or limits, so for a quick rewrite or a simple question, the fast mode is the better call.

CARDS.f: How do you know if an AI tool is good for your task?
CARDS.b: Test it on a few examples where you already know the right answer. Five minutes of that tells you more about how it handles your work than any leaderboard or ad.

CARDS.f: Where does most everyday AI cost come from, and what's next after Foundations?
CARDS.b: Cost tracks tokens, so big pasted inputs and long answers are the expense, trim both (on a monthly plan, they're what use up your limits faster). When you're ready to build with these models, not just chat, the Engineering Mastery course picks up right where this ends.

CARDS.f: What is the chat app quietly doing for you that a builder does themselves?
CARDS.b: Re-sending the whole conversation, adding the hidden system message, and picking and calling the model. Builders do all of it directly through an API, software that hands text to the model and gets text back. That shift, from using a chat app to making the call yourself, is where the Engineering Mastery course begins.

SCENARIOS.title: Is this thing actually thinking?
SCENARIOS.sit: Your aunt just started using a chat assistant and she's a little spooked. "It writes back so fast and it sounds so sure of itself," she says. "Is there a person on the other end? Does it understand me? Is it looking things up?" She's half-convinced it's a tiny genius living in her phone.
SCENARIOS.task: In plain, friendly words, tell your aunt what the AI actually is and how it produces its answers, so she can use it with the right expectations.
SCENARIOS.model: No tiny genius, and no person typing on the other end, but it's still genuinely useful. What she's using is a language model: a program that has read an enormous amount of text and learned the patterns in how words tend to follow one another. When she types a question, it doesn't 'understand' it the way a friend would, and unless the app shows it ran a search (with links to sources), it isn't looking anything up. It's predicting, one chunk at a time, what words would most naturally come next, given everything she wrote plus all the patterns it picked up in training. That's why it can sound so fluent and confident even when it's wrong, because sounding right and being right are two different things to a pattern-predictor. The good news: this makes it fantastic for things like rewriting an email, explaining an idea, or brainstorming, where 'natural and well-phrased' is exactly what you want. Just don't treat its confidence as proof. It's a brilliant writing helper, not an all-knowing oracle.
pts: It's a language model (a program), not a person and not a tiny mind that understands you
It works by predicting likely next words from patterns it learned in training
Unless the app shows it searched (with sources), it isn't looking things up, so confidence is not the same as being correct
It's great for writing, explaining, and brainstorming where good phrasing matters
Use it as a helper, not as an all-knowing source of truth

SCENARIOS.title: The mystery word count
SCENARIOS.sit: A friend keeps hearing the word "tokens" in AI apps, and it's making no sense to her. The app told her a long email she pasted was "about 1,500 tokens," even though it was only about a thousand words. She asks you, a little embarrassed, "What even is a token, and why should I care?"
SCENARIOS.task: Explain what a token is in everyday terms, and give her one practical reason it's worth knowing about.
SCENARIOS.model: Great question, and not embarrassing at all, almost nobody is told this up front. A token is just a small chunk of text the model reads. It's usually not a whole word: it's more like a piece of one. A short common word like 'cat' might be one token, while a longer word like 'unbelievable' might be split into a few pieces ('un', 'believ', 'able'), and spaces and punctuation count too. So 'about a thousand words' can easily come out to well over a thousand tokens, which is exactly what she saw. Why care? Because tokens are the unit everything is measured in: how much text you can send at once, how fast you get an answer, and, if you're on a paid tool, what you're charged. So the practical takeaway is simple: the more text you pour in (long pastes, whole documents) and the longer the answers you ask for, the more tokens, which means slower and pricier. Knowing that, she can keep her pastes and her requests trim when it matters.
pts: A token is a small chunk of text, usually a piece of a word, not a whole word
Spaces and punctuation count, so word count and token count don't match
Tokens are the unit for how much you can send, how fast it is, and what you pay
More text in and longer answers out means more tokens
Practical takeaway: keep pastes and requested answers trim when speed or cost matters

SCENARIOS.title: The assistant that forgot the rules
SCENARIOS.sit: A colleague is using a chat assistant to help plan a big family reunion. Early on he told it the important stuff: the venue holds 80 people, the budget is tight, and his nephew has a serious peanut allergy. After a long back-and-forth, dozens of messages about decorations, music, and timing, he asks it to finalize the food. It cheerfully suggests a peanut-heavy menu, for 150 people, at fancy-restaurant prices. He's upset and says the AI "clearly can't be trusted."
SCENARIOS.task: Your colleague is ready to quit the tool. Explain what really went wrong, and how to use it more reliably, without pretending the AI is smarter than it is.
SCENARIOS.model: Before he quits, it's worth knowing this was predictable, not the AI being flaky. The model can only 'see' a certain amount of recent conversation at once, picture a window that slides along and only holds so much text. That space is the context window. Those crucial early rules, 80 people, tight budget, peanut-free, were said way back at the start of a very long chat, and as the conversation kept growing, the oldest messages slid out of that window (or got buried so deep in a crowded one that the model lost track of them). By the time he asked about food, the model literally no longer had those rules in front of it, so it filled the gaps with normal-sounding guesses. It wasn't ignoring the allergy; it just couldn't see it anymore. The reliable habit: when something really matters, repeat it right where you need it ('finalize the menu for 80 people, tight budget, and absolutely peanut-free'). For a big task, starting a fresh chat with a short summary of the must-haves at the top works even better. And for something safety-critical like an allergy, let the AI draft, but have a human check the final menu. It's a helper, not the last line of defense.
pts: The model only sees a limited window of recent text, the context window
Early instructions slid out of that window as the long conversation grew
It wasn't ignoring the rules; they simply weren't in front of it anymore
Repeat critical details right where they matter, or start fresh with a short summary on top
For safety-critical facts (like an allergy), keep a human checking the final result

SCENARIOS.title: The boring bio
SCENARIOS.sit: A friend is annoyed. He typed "write a bio for my LinkedIn" into a chat assistant and got back something so generic it could describe literally anyone. He's decided the AI "just can't write" and is about to give up on it entirely.
SCENARIOS.task: Without writing the bio for him, explain why the answer came out so bland, and coach him toward a prompt that would actually work.
SCENARIOS.model: The AI can write, it just had nothing to write about. 'Write a bio for my LinkedIn' doesn't tell it who you are, who's reading it, or how you want to sound, so it did the only thing it could and gave you the safe, average, could-be-anyone version. The fix isn't some secret magic phrase. It's giving it a proper brief, the way you'd brief a new assistant on day one. Tell it the facts: your job and how long you've done it, two or three things you're genuinely known for, who it's for (recruiters? clients?), and the vibe you want (warm and human, not stiff corporate-speak). Tell it the shape too, like 'three short sentences, written in first person.' And here's the part people skip: if the first draft is close but a bit off, don't start over, just nudge it ('good, but make it warmer and drop the buzzwords'). Same AI, totally different result, because now it actually knows what you're going for. The rule of thumb: vague question, vague answer; specific question, specific answer.
pts: The bland result came from a vague prompt, not a weak AI
It can't guess details you didn't tell it; it takes your words at face value
Give it the facts: who you are, who it's for, and the tone you want
Spell out the format and length (e.g. 'three short sentences, first person')
Refine with small follow-up nudges instead of starting from scratch

SCENARIOS.title: Where did my conversation go?
SCENARIOS.sit: A colleague spent an hour yesterday in a chat assistant working out a detailed plan for a trip, and it was genuinely helpful, it 'knew' everything they'd discussed. Today they opened the app, started typing in a new chat, and it acted like it had never heard of the trip. They're frustrated and a little worried, convinced the app 'deleted their work' or is broken.
SCENARIOS.task: Reassure your colleague, explain what's actually going on, and tell them how to pick up where they left off.
SCENARIOS.model: Take a breath, nothing's broken and nothing got deleted. Here's the thing that makes it click: the AI has no memory of its own between messages. What felt like 'it knew the trip' yesterday was really the app quietly re-sending the whole conversation back to the model every time you hit enter, so it always had the full thread in front of it. A brand-new chat is a blank page, there's no earlier conversation attached, so today's model genuinely has nothing about the trip to go on. The good news: yesterday's chat almost certainly still exists. Look for a history list or sidebar in the app, open that old conversation, and everything is right there, ready to continue. If you'd rather work in a fresh chat, just bring the context with you: paste a short summary, or copy the key points from yesterday into your first message. (Many apps also have a memory feature, often on by default, that carries a few notes about you across chats. If yours is on, today's chat might recall a detail or two, but it keeps highlights, not the whole conversation, so the old chat is still the place to pick up.) The mental model to keep: each chat is its own self-contained conversation, and the AI only knows what's in the one you're currently in.
pts: The AI has no memory of its own; the app re-sends the whole conversation each time
A brand-new chat is blank, so it knows nothing about an earlier one
Nothing was deleted, the old chat is in the app's history/sidebar; reopen it to continue
To continue in a new chat, paste a short summary or the key points into the first message
A memory feature (often on by default) may carry a few notes across chats, but not the whole conversation

SCENARIOS.title: Sources that look too perfect
SCENARIOS.sit: A student is writing a paper and asked a chat assistant for recent statistics and sources on a fairly niche topic. It gave back exactly what she hoped for: three specific figures, each with a named study, a journal, and a year, all from the last year or two. It looks flawless, and she's about to drop the citations straight into her paper. In passing, she mentions the topic is changing fast right now.
SCENARIOS.task: She asks if she can cite these directly. Explain the two separate risks at play and what to do instead, without telling her the AI is useless.
SCENARIOS.model: Hold on before you cite any of those, there are actually two different traps stacked here. First, hallucination: when you ask for specific stats with named studies and years, the model produces text shaped like real citations, and on a niche topic it will often just invent the details, real-sounding author names, plausible journals, sources that don't actually exist. The fact that it looks flawless is exactly what makes it risky. Second, the knowledge cutoff: a model's training stops at some past date, so it only 'knows' the world up to then. You said this topic is changing fast right now, which means any 'recent' figure could be guessed from an out-of-date picture, and the model usually won't warn you. So the two risks are 'these sources might be made up' and 'this info might be stale', and it sounds equally confident either way. What to do: treat its list as leads, not facts. Search each title and author yourself; if you can't find the real source, don't use it. For anything current, go to an actual up-to-date source, the original studies, a real database, or an AI mode that genuinely searches the web, and even then, open what it cites to confirm each source really says what the AI claims. Lean on the AI to help you understand the topic and draft your writing, just not to be the final word on specific, recent facts.
pts: Two separate risks: made-up sources (hallucination) and stale info (knowledge cutoff)
Specific citations on niche topics are exactly what models invent most convincingly
A model only knows up to its training cutoff, so 'recent' facts can be out of date
Looking flawless is not proof; verify each source actually exists before citing it
For current facts use a real up-to-date source; use the AI to understand and draft, not as the final word

SCENARIOS.title: Right idea, wrong setup
SCENARIOS.sit: A friend tried two things with a chat assistant and struck out both times. First, he took a photo of a printed contract and asked for a summary, and got a vague, partly-wrong answer. Then he asked for today's exchange rate for an upcoming trip, and it confidently gave a number that turned out to be days old. He's ready to declare the whole AI thing "overhyped and useless."
SCENARIOS.task: Talk him off the ledge. Explain in plain terms what went wrong in each case, and tell him how to actually get what he wanted.
SCENARIOS.model: Both of these went sideways for understandable reasons, and neither means AI is useless, he just needs the right setup. The contract photo first: when an app 'reads' a document, it first has to turn it into something the model can take in. Some apps pull out the text, and some also let the model look at each page as a picture. A quick phone snap of a dense printed contract, with glare, an angle, small print, and maybe only some of the pages, gives it a patchy picture at best, so it fills the gaps with guesses, hence the vague, partly-made-up summary. The fix: give it real text (a digital copy you can paste or attach) or clear, well-lit scans of every page, and ask it to quote the exact clauses it's summarizing so you can check them. Now the exchange rate: a plain chat model can't reach the internet on its own and only knows the world up to its training cutoff, so 'today's rate' was a stale guess, not a live lookup. The fix: use an app or mode that actually searches the web, and check it really did (look for a link or source it cites), or honestly, for a live rate, just glance at a finance site. The real lesson isn't 'AI is unreliable.' It's that abilities like reading images and searching the web are extra tools a given app may or may not have, so match the setup to the task and both of these become easy.
pts: Reading a file means the app converts it first; a quick photo of dense pages gives it a patchy picture to work from
Fix for the contract: give it real text or clear scans of every page, and ask it to quote the clauses
A plain chat model can't browse the web and is frozen at its cutoff, so 'today's rate' was a stale guess
Fix for the rate: use an app/mode that actually searches, and check it cited a source
Image-reading and web search are extra tools an app may or may not have; match the setup to the task

SCENARIOS.title: Using the Ferrari for everything
SCENARIOS.sit: A new coworker just discovered AI and is using the biggest, most powerful (and priciest) model, with its deepest thinking setting switched on, for absolutely everything, quick "can you reword this" messages, casual brainstorming, and also dumping in huge documents for long detailed summaries. He's proud of always picking 'the best one,' but the team's bill is creeping up and the quick little tasks feel weirdly slow. He asks you, sincerely, if he's doing it right.
SCENARIOS.task: Without overwhelming him, give him a simple habit for choosing a model, keeping cost sane, and knowing when to double-check the answer.
SCENARIOS.model: Love the instinct to do good work, let's just right-size it, because 'always the most powerful model' is costing you speed and money you don't need to spend. Two quick questions before any task will sort almost all of this out. First: how hard is this, really? A quick reword or a casual brainstorm doesn't need the heavyweight, a smaller, faster, cheaper model handles those beautifully and feels snappier. Save the big one for genuinely tricky, high-stakes work. The same goes for that deep thinking setting: it's brilliant for genuinely hard, multi-step problems, but on a quick reword it just makes you wait. Second: what happens if it's wrong? For low-stakes, throwaway stuff, move fast and accept good-enough. For anything that matters, use the stronger model, give it real sources, and check the output yourself. On the creeping bill: cost mostly tracks how much text goes in and out, and your big drivers are exactly the things you mentioned, dumping in huge documents (lots of text in) and asking for long detailed answers (lots of text out). Trim the pastes to the part that actually matters and ask for shorter summaries, and you'll watch the cost drop. And one habit that prevents most mistakes: trust it to draft, brainstorm, and reword, but double-check it on facts, numbers, recent events, and anything it cites. Do that and you're using it like a pro. And if you ever want to go further, building this into real tools, wiring it into your own apps, controlling cost at scale, that's exactly what the Engineering Mastery course picks up next.
pts: Right-size it: small/fast/cheap for easy tasks, the powerful model and deep thinking only for hard, high-stakes work
Two quick questions: how hard is this, and what happens if it's wrong?
Cost mostly tracks text in and out; big pastes and long answers are the bill, so trim both
Trust it to draft, brainstorm, and reword; double-check facts, numbers, recent events, and citations
